a168.speaker: One resident of al-Fashir (anonymous)
a168.speech: Told Reuters: "The RSF's artillery and drones are shelling al-Fashir morning and night." He added that electricity was completely shut down, bakeries were closed and medical supplies were scarce. ; "The number of people dying has increased every day and the cemeteries are expanding."

a168.speaker: Analysts
a168.speech: Say the city's fall could pave the way for what would be Sudan's de facto division.

a168.speaker: Monitors
a168.speech: Say the camps in which many displaced people are living are already in famine.

a168.speaker: One doctor in al-Fashir (anonymous, asked not to be named for her safety)
a168.speech: Said hunger was an even bigger problem than the shelling: "The children are malnourished, the adults are malnourished. Even today, I haven't had any breakfast because I can't find anything."

a168.speaker: Locals in al-Fashir
a168.speech: Said the RSF has blocked food supplies and that aid convoys trying to reach the city have been attacked.

a168.speaker: Residents of al-Fashir
a168.speech: Told Reuters that many people have resorted to eating hay or ambaz, a type of animal feed made out of peanut shells.

a168.speaker: One advocacy group
a168.speech: Said even ambaz was running out.

a168.speaker: Rapid Support Forces (RSF)
a168.speech: Did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

a168.speaker: Residents who fled to Tawila
a168.speech: Some of those who made it told Reuters that groups of RSF fighters attacked them along the way.

a168.speaker: Enaam Abdallah, 19-year-old who fled al-Fashir
a168.speech: "We fled to Shagra (village) first before getting to Tawila and they attacked us again." ; "If they find your phone, they take it. Money, they take it. A donkey or anything, they'll take it. They killed people in front of us and kidnapped girls in front of us."

a168.speaker: Emergency Lawyers, a human rights group
a168.speech: Said on Monday that at least 14 people fleeing al-Fashir were killed and dozens injured when they were attacked in a village along the route.

a168.speaker: People who arrived in Tawila
a168.speech: Told Reuters they receive small amounts of grain, including sorghum and rice, but the amounts vary and are insufficient.

a168.speaker: Médecins Sans Frontières spokesperson
a168.speech: Told Reuters that since mid-June the aid group has treated 2,500 cases of cholera.

a168.speaker: Coordinating Committee for Displaced People, a Sudanese advocacy group
a168.speech: According to the group, some 52 people have died from cholera.

a168.speaker: Norwegian Refugee Council (assessment)
a168.speech: An assessment found that only 10% of people in Tawila had reliable access to water, and even fewer had access to latrines; most families report eating one meal a day or less, the organisation said.

a168.speaker: Huda Ali, mother-of-four displaced in Tawila
a168.speech: "We don't have houses to protect us from the rain and we don't have tarps. We have to wait for the rain to stop for the children to sleep." She said she tried to make sure her children washed their hands and only ate food that had been properly heated.

a168.speaker: United Nations
a168.speech: Called for a humanitarian pause to fighting in al-Fashir last month as the rainy season began.

a168.speaker: Rapid Support Forces (RSF)
a168.speech: Rejected the United Nations' call for a humanitarian pause.

a325.speaker: UK government
a325.speech: Said in February it would slash foreign aid spending by 40% - from 0.5% of gross national income to 0.3% - to increase defence spending to 2.5% after pressure from the US.

a325.speaker: UK government
a325.speech: Said spending on multilateral aid bodies - money given to international organisations like the World Bank - would be protected, including the Gavi vaccine alliance, and said the UK would also continue to play a key humanitarian role in hotspots such as Gaza, Ukraine and Sudan.

a325.speaker: UK government
a325.speech: Said the cuts follow “a line-by-line strategic review of aid” by the minister, which focused on “prioritisation, efficiency, protecting planned humanitarian support and live contracts while ensuring responsible exit from programming where necessary”.

a325.speaker: Foreign Office report and impact assessment
a325.speech: Show the biggest cuts this year will come in Africa, with less spent on women’s health and water sanitation with increased risks, it says, of disease and death.

a325.speaker: Aid charities
a325.speech: Have criticised the move, saying the cuts would impact the world’s most vulnerable people.

a325.speaker: Baroness Chapman, UK minister for development
a325.speech: “Every pound must work harder for UK taxpayers and the people we help around the world and these figures show how we are starting to do just that through having a clear focus and priorities.”

a325.speaker: Foreign Office
a325.speech: Said bilateral support - aid going directly to the recipient country - for some countries would decrease and multilateral organisations deemed to be underperforming would face future funding cuts.

a325.speaker: Sarah Champion, chair of the International Development Committee
a325.speech: Said it appears the cuts “will come at the expense of some of the world’s most vulnerable people”.

a440.speaker: Antonio Guterres, UN Secretary-General
a440.speech: "Nearly one million people are displaced and require urgent help, especially during this rainy season," noting that releasing money from the CERF is one of the fastest ways to ensure aid reaches those who need it the most.

a440.speaker: Antonio Guterres, UN Secretary-General
a440.speech: Said that under the leadership of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, new measures to bring unity and reconciliation have spurred great enthusiasm within the country and the enthusiastic support of the international community ; "However, the impact of inter-communal tensions presents a challenge for the new leadership. It is critical to act immediately."

a503.speaker: Ms Paulina Majogoro, National Council of NGOs (NaCoNGO) Leader in Geita Region
a503.speech: Shared the report during the annual regional NGOs meeting, saying the challenge results from policy changes, economic crises, or shifts in donor priorities ; "Here in Geita, more than 10 projects have been affected, including the suspension of essential services such as the PEPFAR HIV prevention program, anti-malaria campaigns, and basic healthcare services" ; explained that the situation has exposed a lack of alternative local funding sources, resulting in NGOs becoming overly dependent on external donors, often leading to complete collapse when donor policies change.

a503.speaker: Mr Deusdedith Kayango, Planning and Coordination Administrative Officer
a503.speech: Urged NGOs to focus on priority groups and projects to avoid misuse or unnecessary expenditure of donor funds ; stressed that all NGOs are responsible for aligning with government priorities and implementing projects effectively so that their interventions can have a visible and direct impact on community well-being.

a503.speaker: Mr Martha Kaloso, Assistant Community Development Officer for Geita Region
a503.speech: Said that the region currently has 70 NGOs operating across its five districts in various sectors, including education and health ; acknowledged that NGOs have significantly contributed to raising community awareness on environmental conservation, combating gender-based violence, and abandoning oppressive customs and traditions.

a740.speaker: Donald Trump, incoming US President
a740.speech: Has expressed skepticism toward trade agreements; during his first term, advocated for reducing foreign aid.

a740.speaker: BBC (report cited)
a740.speech: Reported that Trump's previous administration hinted at reducing U.S. involvement in the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA).

a740.speaker: US Biden administration
a740.speech: Viewed the War and Economic Crimes Court (WECC) in Liberia as crucial to strengthening Liberia's democratic systems, as it would address issues of accountability and justice in the postwar nation; support for the WECC was part of broader U.S. efforts to enhance Liberia's institutions, with development aid targeting governance reforms rather than purely economic interests.

a740.speaker: Liberian Observer (cited)
a740.speech: Cited as the source that President Boakai's bid for a non-permanent seat on the United Nations Security Council is one of Liberia's most ambitious diplomatic goals in recent years.

a861.speaker: Bheki 'Rubber' Simelane, former President of Mbabane Highlanders FC
a861.speech: Opposed the move to change the club's name and has since escalated the matter to court, having signed an 18-month management contract with the team two months before the unveiling.

a861.speaker: Pat Vilakati, Chief Executive Officer of the Premier League of Eswatini (PLE)
a861.speech: Confirmed that while four other clubs' name change proposals were adopted, that of the Ernest Mavuso-led side was not ; Said the change is pending, explaining that name changes are generally handled by the football's mother body, the Eswatini Football Association (EFA), before being adopted by the PLE Board of Governors ; He mentioned that the name Mbabane Highlanders FC would be maintained in all fixtures too.

a913.speaker: Hassan Abdi Robleh, Prefect of Dikhil
a913.speech: After a welcome message, gave an overview of the various projects carried out by USAID in his region before speaking of the region’s tourism opportunities.

a913.speaker: Nancy Ostrowski, USAID Representative in Djibouti
a913.speech: Emphasised the commitment of the American people to supporting the development process of the regional local authorities.

a913.speaker: Abdallah Mohamed Hassan, interim President of the Regional Council of Dikhil
a913.speech: Thanked the American people and USAID for the valuable donation and in particular for their support to local development initiatives: “This equipment is of crucial importance in strengthening our capacity to serve the community,” he declared. It is, he continued, “another step towards a better future for our region, where civil society will play a key role.”

a946.speaker: Benedicto Kondowe, National Advocacy Platform (NAP) chairperson
a946.speech: says the Citizen Manifesto currently under formulation is set to improve participatory democracy by ensuring that political authority is derived from the people and not political parties' interests; said once completed, the Citizen Manifesto will capture citizen aspirations on the kind of government and leadership they would like to see beyond 2025 ; “This initiative is centred around participatory democracy. If you look at Section 12 of the Malawi Constitution, legal and political authority is derived from the people of Malawi.” ; “But what we have seen in practice is that political parties determine what Malawians want and this initiative seeks to turn around that narrative.” ; said the Citizen Manifesto will enable political parties to respond to Malawians aspirations and leadership needs as reflected in the blueprint, a framework that will show whether political parties are aligned or not.

a946.speaker: Robert White, Tilitonse Foundation chief executive officer
a946.speech: In his key note address, challenged the stakeholders to think beyond elections: “There is a new world order developing and things are changing like the cutting of foreign aid, an issue that people are concerned about. This is an opportunity to put our agenda forward to shape the future we want.”

a946.speaker: Robert White, Tilitonse Foundation chief executive officer
a946.speech: warned the civil society against compromising themselves by being active political players.

a1165.speaker: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (UNOCHA) (recent report)
a1165.speech: According to UNOCHA's recent report that came out a week ago, there are currently 2.4 million internally displaced persons in Ethiopia. It is higher than war-torn Yemen and constitutes about 2.4pc of Ethiopia's entire population.

a1165.speaker: Abiy Ahmed's administration
a1165.speech: Does not refute the numbers, but neither is it seeing it for the socio-economic devastation it is.

a1165.speaker: Oromia Disaster & Risk Management Commission
a1165.speech: According to the Commission, 400,000 internally displaced persons from the towns along the administrative demarcation of the Oromia and Somali regional states were recently returned.

a1165.speaker: United States Agency for International Development (USAID)
a1165.speech: Has since suspended food aid for displaced persons in the southern regional state due to what it said was violence, even after acknowledging that doing as such would affect 140,000 people.

a1315.speaker: World Bank Group
a1315.speech: Has now officially labelled Namibia a lower-middle-income country, down from its previous classification as an upper-middle-income country, based on Gross National Income (GNI) per capita expressed in US dollars according to the Atlas method.

a1315.speaker: Mally Likukela, economist
a1315.speech: Pointed out that eligibility for a wider pool of Official Development Assistance will boil down to how these ODAs are used. "The downgrade confirms that Namibia is now formally caught in the middle-income country trap. This is a worrying phenomenon because it suggests the country suffers from a policy misdiagnosis syndrome. The misdiagnosis is what explains the reason why the country failed to lift itself out of the upper-middle-income category despite the implementation of the famous NDP5, HPPs, etc."

a1315.speaker: Mally Likukela, economist
a1315.speech: Continued that another important aspect is that the new classification shows how the World Bank views Namibia, as this is how they will position their strategies towards the country. "The question is, does Namibia accept this view as the true reflection of the situation on the ground? This classification also has serious implications for the country's development roadmap. The soon-to-be-launched NDP6 is based on the old category, and all strategies were informed by that category, and now with this new classification, NDP6 needs to be recalibrated to reflect the new worldview of the country."

a1315.speaker: Klaus Schade, economic analyst
a1315.speech: Said the reclassification means every Namibian has, on average, become poorer. "This is not surprising since we experienced lower economic growth rates and a higher-than-expected population growth rate. Hence, the GNI is divided among a larger population, resulting in lower per capita income. However, we can safely assume the drop in income has not affected everyone equally but affected low-income earners in particular." ; Added this development from the World Bank drives Namibia further away from Vision 2030, which envisages the country to be an industrialised country, which he noted would be synonymous with a high-income country ; "It signals to potential investors that the purchasing power has declined, which might impact the investment decisions of those who aim at the local market. We might have access to concessional loans with more preferential conditions or grants, but that is certainly not the objective of our economic policies and development plans."

a1315.speaker: Eben De Klerk, analyst
a1315.speech: "Politicians will no doubt celebrate this failure, for we can potentially now borrow more at cheaper rates. The bottom line is that this downgrade simply reflects the government's failure to stimulate economic growth and job creation. In fact, government keeps moving in the opposite direction, with laws and policies hampering investment and private sector growth. Instead of celebrating, our leaders should bow their heads in shame."

a1315.speaker: World Bank
a1315.speech: Pointed out that in 2024, Namibia's GDP grew 3.7%, a 0.7-point deceleration from 2023. "Inflation (based on the GDP deflator) slowed from 6.6% in 2023 to 3.3% in 2024. One of the main factors behind the slower GDP growth was a sharp deceleration in mining and quarrying, for which growth went from +19.3% in 2023 to -1.2% in 2024 due to weak demand for diamonds." The institution also adjusted Namibia's population data upwards, leading to a 12.9% decrease in the Atlas GNI per capita.

a1315.speaker: Hage Geingob, late President of Namibia
a1315.speech: Often reiterated a call for Namibia's income level to be reclassified, arguing the classification as an upper middle-income country was insensitive to distortions created by the unequal distribution of resources ; constantly highlighted that the classification has serious implications for Namibia's access to affordable debt financing and grants.

a1371.speaker: Johan Coetzee, Managing Director of Rössing Uranium
a1371.speech: "This includes N$38 million allocated to the Rössing Foundation and N$23 million towards community initiatives."

a1371.speaker: Johan Coetzee, Managing Director of Rössing Uranium
a1371.speech: Said the change from owner-operated mining to a contractor-mining model, with Beifang Mining Technology Services Namibia taking over operations, aimed to secure the mine's future beyond 2026 and provide new opportunities for skills development.

a1371.speaker: Gaudentia Kröhne, Deputy Minister of Mines and Energy of Namibia
a1371.speech: Commended the mine's continued contribution to national development: "The footprint of Rössing Uranium in the fulfilment of this vision has been remarkable", citing the recent construction of a N$23 million police station in Swakopmund's DRC settlement.

a1371.speaker: Gaudentia Kröhne, Deputy Minister of Mines and Energy of Namibia
a1371.speech: Added that uranium accounted for 26,3% of Namibia's total export earnings in February 2025, and said: "Its impact must extend beyond the balance sheet and translate into meaningful benefits for ordinary Namibians."

a1371.speaker: Rössing Uranium 2024 Sustainability and Performance Report
a1371.speech: Cited as the source of the reported figures, released at the report's official launch in Windhoek on Tuesday: total material mined rose by 82% compared to 2023; capital investment exceeded N$1,1 billion; total assets rose 22% to N$10,1 billion; local procurement spend increased to N$4,37 billion, representing 84% of total procurement expenditure; community development spending rose to N$61,6 million; revenue declined 9% to N$5,93 billion and net profit after tax dropped from N$1,34 billion to N$1,03 billion; the company recorded a fatality at a solar construction project, ending a 19-year fatality-free period.

a1414.speaker: National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) report
a1414.speech: Reported zero coffee export in the first nine months of 2024.

a1414.speaker: Precedence Research (market research company)
a1414.speech: Reported that the global coffee market size was worth about 245.2 billion Dollars in 2024 and is expected to reach around 381.52 billion Dollars by 2034, growing at a CAGR of 4.51% from 2024 to 2034.

a1414.speaker: Centre for Agricultural and Biosciences International (CABI)
a1414.speech: "Of the total hectarage put to coffee originally in Nigeria only about 20% is currently effective." It further stated that "most of the farmers are small farmers having between 0-4 hectares of land."

a1414.speaker: Yunnan Coffee Association
a1414.speech: Reports that over 95% of the country's coffee production is from the province.

a1546.speaker: Daniel Chapo, President of Mozambique
a1546.speech: Said the state should not accept continuing to receive "inferior revenues" from the mining of resources and criticised the lack of basic services in areas where megaprojects are being exploited: "We shouldn't continue to have communities in large project areas always clamouring for quality schools and health centres or other living conditions. Our passage through Tete, Palma [Cabo Delgado] and Inhambane shows this reality. Nor should we accept that the Mozambican state receives lower revenues for resources that are its sovereignty."

a1546.speaker: Daniel Chapo, President of Mozambique
a1546.speech: Emphasised that Mozambique is a country rich in strategic resources, including arable land, water resources, a large exclusive economic zone and soil and subsoil riches, advocating "bold decisions" to ensure that the resources serve the country's economic and social development: "It's up to our generation to break the cycle of imbalances that perpetuate dependence on foreign aid. We urgently need to change the prevailing extractive model that has been in place until now. Only in this way will we achieve the economic independence that is at the heart of our governance", advocating the training of human resources to control the exploitation of resources and their application in Mozambique's industrialisation.

a1546.speaker: Daniel Chapo, President of Mozambique
a1546.speech: Asked the executive leader of the Office for the Coordination of Reforms and Strategic Projects for actions and partnerships to speed up the country's economic and social development: "This Office must be a catalyst for profound changes in our economy and society. We need to change the current reality, rooted in our colonial heritage, in which our economy is still centred on the export of raw materials and logistics corridors."

a1546.speaker: Conta Cidadao (Citizen's Account) 2023 report, Ministry of Economy and Finance (cited, via Lusa)
a1546.speech: States that in 2023 the Mozambican state transferred more than 77.1 million meticais (1.1 million euros) to community development programmes with resources obtained from mining and oil extraction, funding for local projects stemming from the "social responsibility of mining and oil companies"; the community of Nyamanhumbir, Montepuez district, received the most with 21,405,750 meticais (322,500 euros), while 15,260,670 meticais (230,000 euros) went to Benga in Moatize district and 7,333,680 meticais (110,500 euros) to Pande in Govuro district.

a1597.speaker: United Nations World Food Programme (WFP)
a1597.speech: has announced a $3.6 million (over GH₵58.3 million) contribution from the United States and the United Kingdom to provide emergency food and nutrition assistance to 70,000 people impacted by drought in northern Ghana.

a1597.speaker: Aurore Rusiga, WFP Country Director
a1597.speech: expressed gratitude for the timely support: "With staple food prices rising beyond the reach of most families, this contribution is a lifeline for Ghanaian families in need."

a1597.speaker: Kimberly Rosen, USAID/Ghana Mission Director
a1597.speech: highlighted the significance of the partnership: "This collaboration underscores our shared commitment to supporting vulnerable Ghanaians during crises. The United States will continue to stand with Ghana in addressing climate-related challenges."

a1597.speaker: Richard Sandall, UK Development Director to Ghana
a1597.speech: "This assistance is vital to safeguard the nutrition, assets, and recovery of thousands of families in Northern Ghana. The UK remains committed to supporting Ghana's climate resilience and food security efforts in collaboration with the government and other stakeholders."

a1778.speaker: Kiel Institute for the World Economy (report)
a1778.speech: A report by the famous Kiel Institute for the World Economy states that if Donald Trump cuts American aid to Ukraine, Europe will have to double its support if it wants to preserve Kyiv.

a1778.speaker: Germany (government pledge)
a1778.speech: Announced that it is allocating 11 billion euros to Ukraine.

a1793.speaker: Christos Stylianides, European Commissioner for Humanitarian Aid and Crisis Management
a1793.speech: "More than a quarter of a million people have fled their homes. The reception capacities of neighbouring countries are stretched to the extreme and the situation in Tanzania is particularly worrying." ; according to his statement, the additional funds granted by the EU will help to provide essential assistance to people in need and to improve the living conditions of refugees, notably in Tanzania.

a1793.speaker: European Commission (announcement)
a1793.speech: Announced on 31 May additional humanitarian aid of 10 million euros to assist the growing numbers of displaced Burundians, an envelope that comes on top of the 12.2 million euros already mobilised since the beginning of the year, "which brings to 22 million euros the humanitarian aid provided in 2016 by the EU in the framework of the Burundian crisis."

a1793.speaker: European Union (assessment)
a1793.speech: For the EU, even though additional camps have been opened (at Mtendeli and Nduta) to cope with the incessant flow of refugees, it is necessary to improve living conditions in the camps: "The risks of infections and epidemics are high. The accommodation conditions expose the most vulnerable to significant risks."

a1834.speaker: United Nations founding charter (document)
a1834.speech: Articulated a hopeful vision: "To save succeeding generations from the scourge of war, to affirm faith in fundamental human rights and to promote social progress and better standards of life in larger freedom."

a1834.speaker: Annalisa Bareback, President of the United Nations General Assembly
a1834.speech: Opening the historic meeting, declared the anniversary a "make or break moment for the institution"; dismissed suggestions that the UN is obsolete, arguing instead that the organisation falters when member States fail to act in accordance with the charter, insisting it is as strong as its members and urging accountability for those who violate international norms; highlighted concrete achievements, noting programmes that educate millions of children and the World Food Programme's efforts to feed vulnerable populations worldwide.

a1834.speaker: United Nations Secretary-General
a1834.speech: Framed the choice before leaders in stark terms, saying the UN's creation was a conscious decision — cooperation over chaos, law over lawlessness and collective responsibility over raw self-interest — and warned that the world has entered an era of reckless disruption and relentless human suffering, with leaders having to decide whether to embrace a future governed by laws and cooperation or one dominated by power struggles and impunity; argued that human rights are not ornamental but constitute the bedrock of peace and require persistent defence and political will; said the Sustainable Development Goals remain the roadmap for shared progress but their success depends on adequate financing and sustained commitments, with recent cuts to aid risking the reversal of hard-won gains in health, education and poverty reduction.

a1834.speaker: United Nations Secretary-General
a1834.speech: On Sudan, condemned the slaughter and starvation of civilians and called for an immediate end to external support that fuels the bloodshed; demanded a full ceasefire and a just, lasting peace.

a1834.speaker: United Nations Secretary-General
a1834.speech: On Gaza, lamented a conflict entering its third year, with unprecedented levels of death and destruction in his tenure; while reiterating condemnation of the attacks of October 7, 2023 and the taking of hostages, emphasised that nothing can justify collective punishment or the systematic destruction of civilian life and infrastructure.

a2020.speaker: Moussa Faki Mahamat, President of the African Union (AU)
a2020.speech: Today accused Israel of a "massive massacre of Palestinians," following the deaths of more than 100 people during a humanitarian aid delivery, which local authorities attributed to the Israelis.

a2020.speaker: Moussa Faki Mahamat, Chairperson of the African Union Commission
a2020.speech: Declared today at the United Nations that "it is a great mistake to think that the world is safe while Africa lacks protection against the virus."

a2020.speaker: Moussa Faki Mahamat, Chairperson of the African Union Commission
a2020.speech: Considers that democracy in Africa faces "enormous problems" and that, in many countries, elections have gone from being the solution to becoming the problem.

a2020.speaker: Moussa Faki Mahamat, Chairperson of the African Union Commission
a2020.speech: Today defended the "imperative necessity" for Africa to break its dependence on the outside world, adding that the COVID-19 pandemic served as a "deafening" reminder of that urgency.

a2020.speaker: Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) member countries
a2020.speech: Agreed to promote an increase in COVID-19 screening tests and to create humanitarian corridors for medical teams.

a2020.speaker: African Union (AU)
a2020.speech: Announced today that it will support with 350,000 dollars the emergency response for the populations affected by the passage of Cyclone Idai in Mozambique, Zimbabwe and Malawi, which caused at least 300 deaths.

a2052.speaker: South African authorities
a2052.speech: After the terrorist attack, assured the Owambo representatives of immediate measures to defend the border and to pursue those responsible.

a2052.speaker: Responsible South African military service authorities
a2052.speech: It cannot yet be learned with certainty from them which group was involved in the retaliatory attack.

a2052.speaker: Anwar Sadat, President of Egypt
a2052.speech: Warned America of the dangers of supplying Israel with certain categories of weapons; said in a television interview that the delivery of these weapons would bring with it a similar escalation on Egypt's part, and gave to understand that he would turn to the Soviet Union if Washington continued the weapons deliveries to Israel.

a2052.speaker: American press reports
a2052.speech: According to them, the USA is to supply F-16 fighter aircraft and missiles with which Arab capitals could be hit.

a2052.speaker: Francisco Costa Gomes, President of Portugal
a2052.speech: Issued an appeal to the population to hand in their weapons by Friday; instructed the troops to open fire on any person using weapons against citizens, police officers or soldiers; and promised persons in illegal possession of weapons that they would not be prosecuted if they handed the weapons in before Friday of this week.

a2052.speaker: A radically left-wing Portuguese officer
a2052.speech: Announced in a radio address that he had distributed more than 1,000 automatic weapons to revolutionary workers; he has since left his unit and gone into hiding.

a2052.speaker: Spokesman for the left-wing 'Militia' (anonymous)
a2052.speech: Gave to understand that the government's demand to hand over the weapons was directed against the left-wing groups: “We used our weapons against the fascist regime that was overthrown in April 1974, and we will not hand over our weapons until the working class has come to the helm.”

a2052.speaker: Valéry Giscard d'Estaing, President of France
a2052.speech: Gave to understand that differences in the interpretation of détente were the reason for the postponement of the talks with Brezhnev; he is optimistic and added that a document on French-Soviet political cooperation would be signed today.

a2052.speaker: Pastor Titus Haita, acting Chief Minister of Owambo
a2052.speech: Paid tribute to the sacrifice that the sons of Owambo made at the border – the seven tribal policemen killed in the attack, as well as the sub-headman and a woman – and assured the inhabitants of Owambo that public order would be maintained by a determined government.

a2052.speaker: J. B. Vorster, South African Prime Minister (message read out at the funeral)
a2052.speech: Expressed his regret about the incident in a peaceful country that does not interfere in the affairs of its neighbours.

a2052.speaker: J. de Wet, Commissioner-General for the Indigenous Peoples of South West Africa
a2052.speech: Addressed the population of Owambo in his own name and said that it could not be permitted for the peace to be disturbed by a small group of troublemakers and tyrants from outside the country's borders.

a2052.speaker: Dirk Mudge, Member of the Executive Committee
a2052.speech: Expressed himself optimistically in London regarding further talks with British diplomats; considers a meeting with German Foreign Minister Hans-Dietrich Genscher towards the end of the week unlikely, since relations between the West German and South African governments are somewhat strained; and added that because of the short notice of the trip a meeting cannot be arranged everywhere even where government representatives are willing.

a2052.speaker: Dr Carel de Wet, South African Ambassador
a2052.speech: Said in his welcoming address that the constitutional conference in the Turnhalle was proof of the multinational character of the peoples of South West Africa, and that through the delegates' visit abroad the world must take note that the diverse peoples of South West Africa are determined to live together in peace and harmony ; described the delegates' visit to the USA, England and West Germany as a “golden opportunity” to consider aspects of world politics in a larger framework.

a2052.speaker: Spokesmen for the South West African delegates
a2052.speech: In their first interview in London, again expressed the wish that South Africa must above all, during the negotiating period of the constitutional conference, ensure law and order in South West Africa.

a2052.speaker: Dr B. J. Africa, leader of the Rehoboth Baster Council
a2052.speech: Stressed that their views had been heard in many places, but that it could not be determined to what extent their arguments had been accepted; said the delegation started out at a disadvantage because SWAPO had for years propagated a different policy for South West Africa, and that the trip served above all to present the other side of the situation without courting cheap sympathy; asked whether the conference's declaration of intent amounted to recognition of South African bantustan policy, he replied that it rather appeared as though the present constitutional development was moving away from that concept.

a2054.speaker: Elon Musk, Tesla CEO and U.S. special government employee
a2054.speech: In a tweet made on Sunday said Malema committed a serious crime and should be punished accordingly, and has called for immediate sanctions against Malema: “Immediate sanctions for Malema and declaration of him as an international criminal!”

a2054.speaker: The White House
a2054.speech: According to the White House, Musk is officially serving under President Donald Trump as a special government employee.

a2054.speaker: Julius Malema, South African politician and Economic Freedom Fighters leader
a2054.speech: “We have taken a decision that we are going to remove the mayor of PE [Port Elizabeth]” ; “Why? Why not [mayor of DA-led Johannesburg Herman] Mashaba, why not Solly [Msimanga – mayor of DA-led Tshwane]? Because the mayor of DA in PE is a white man. So, these people, when you want to hit them hard – go after a white man. They feel a terrible pain, because you have touched a white man.” ; “But we are starting with this whiteness. We are cutting the throat of whiteness. Trollip will not be a mayor after the 6th of April, if they give us that date.”

a2054.speaker: Donald Trump, U.S. President
a2054.speech: Earlier announced plans to cut off all future funding to South Africa, citing concerns over “land expropriation and alleged discriminatory treatment” of some residents, particularly foreigners in the country; the announcement was shared on his Truth Social account following South African President Cyril Ramaphosa's signing of an expropriation bill into law.

a2054.speaker: Cyril Ramaphosa, President of South Africa
a2054.speech: In response, clarified that South Africa receives no funding from the US except for PEPFAR aid, which supports the country's HIV/AIDS programme.

a2162.speaker: National Strategic Plan for Digital Health of Mali (PSNSN) 2024-2028 (document)
a2162.speech: According to the plan, digital health has encouraged the use of information technologies in the management of medical records, therapeutic decision-making and the creation of care plans in order to respond effectively to patients' needs; the plan's estimated cost for the period is 32 million euros, about 21 billion CFA francs, and it comprises 17 political, methodological and implementation recommendations, insisting on the need to strengthen the skills of teams both in management and in the field.

a2162.speaker: Colonel Assa Badiallo Toure, Malian Minister of Health and Social Development
a2162.speech: Said this technological progress brings many advantages to our facilities and enables rapid and effective access to health care for patients; to that end, the country, in its drive for innovation through a digital transformation strategy, intends to digitalise all systems in the health sector by 2030 - an ambitious challenge, but one that can be met.

a2162.speaker: Colonel Assa Badiallo Toure, Malian Minister of Health and Social Development
a2162.speech: Said the Plan, which aims to improve access to primary and specialised health care, is "an essential lever to modernise our health system and respond to the needs of the Malian people."

a2330.speaker: Gabriel Degbegni, coordinator of the MCA-Benin II programme
a2330.speech: Reported at the opening of the proceedings that the past three months of implementation of MCA-Benin II projects end with a commitment rate of about "51%" and a disbursement rate of "more than 70%", figures "clearly improved compared with previous quarters", and that since the programme began the commitment and disbursement rates of financial resources are assessed at "86% and 48%" respectively.

a2330.speaker: Gabriel Degbegni, coordinator of the MCA-Benin II programme
a2330.speech: Announced the completion of certain power line works for December 2021 and of several electrical substations for the first quarter of 2022, but said certain works would be delayed owing to difficulties on the ground - the harmful effects of Covid-19, the poor performance of certain companies, the weak responsiveness of stakeholders and numerous modifications to the initial scope of works - affecting the substations to be built at Vedoko, Maria-Gleta, Bohicon, Parakou, Djougou and Natitingou, now expected in the second half of 2022.

a2330.speaker: Gabriel Degbegni, coordinator of the MCA-Benin II programme
a2330.speech: Drew the board of directors' attention to the challenges to be met regarding the continued implementation of off-grid electricity access projects: "I know that the national coordination will continue to benefit from your support in meeting these challenges, and from your valuable guidance and recommendations with a view to completing all planned activities on time."

a2501.speaker: The New York Times
a2501.speech: Reported on Friday that the Trump administration wants to reduce the staff of USAID to fewer than 300 people, down from more than 10,000 currently, a cut of 97%; said the few staff spared from the layoffs work in health and humanitarian assistance, citing three sources familiar with the plan who spoke on condition of anonymity; added that USAID officials were informed that around 800 programmes and contracts administered by the agency were being cancelled; and reported that two unions representing USAID staff launched legal action on Thursday seeking an injunction to halt the dismissals and forced administrative leave of employees.

a2501.speaker: Three sources familiar with the reduction plan (anonymous)
a2501.speech: Told the New York Times that the few personnel spared from the layoffs work in health and humanitarian assistance.

a2501.speaker: Two unions representing USAID staff
a2501.speech: Argue that the dismantling of USAID cannot be carried out without the approval of Congress.

a2501.speaker: US State Department
a2501.speech: Did not immediately respond to AFP's request for comment.

a2501.speaker: Elon Musk
a2501.speech: Described USAID as a "viper's nest of Marxists (...) who hate America."

a2501.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a2501.speech: Had said last week that USAID was run by "a bunch of radical lunatics."

a2501.speaker: USAID (note posted on its website)
a2501.speech: "On Friday, February 7, 2025, at 11:59 p.m. (EST) (Saturday 04:59 GMT), all personnel directly employed by USAID will be placed on administrative leave worldwide," with the exception of staff deemed essential; the note adds that employees working abroad and their families have 30 days to return to the United States.

a2567.speaker: Cristian Munduate, UNICEF Representative in Nigeria
a2567.speech: “This emergency support from IHS Nigeria comes at a critical time when thousands of children and families are facing enormous hardship” ; “Our longstanding partnership with IHS Nigeria has always prioritized reaching the most vulnerable communities. Together, we have made strides in strengthening primary healthcare systems, education, and child protection. Today’s renewed collaboration ensures that the children of Mokwa are not left behind.”

a2567.speaker: UNICEF (statement)
a2567.speech: According to the statement by UNICEF, through this joint response, more than 30,000 displaced people and community members are expected to benefit from access to safe water, improved sanitation and better primary healthcare services, while children will regain access to education and critical child protection services.

a2567.speaker: Mohamad Darwish, CEO, IHS Nigeria
a2567.speech: “At IHS Nigeria, we are driven by the belief that communities must not only survive disastrous incidents, but emerge stronger from them. Our partnership with UNICEF is a proven model for helping deliver sustainable impact in some of Nigeria’s most vulnerable regions.” ; “We have supported similar interventions across other communities impacted by natural disasters, and by working together once again in Mokwa, we are helping deliver access to water, health services, and dignity for families who need it most.”

a2634.speaker: Donald Trump, President of the United States (executive orders)
a2634.speech: Signed approximately 78 executive orders, including the step of the United States withdrawing from the World Health Organisation (WHO) and suspending development aid outside the United States for a period of 90 days.

a2634.speaker: Reports (unnamed)
a2634.speech: Reports claim that some USAID staff who are American citizens may be sent home.

a2634.speaker: Samia Suluhu Hassan, President of Tanzania
a2634.speech: In her speech at the launch of the Fifth National Multisectoral Strategic Framework for HIV/AIDS Control (NMSF V) on 1 December 2022 in Lindi region, called on leaders of various sectors, including the 15 ministers who were present, to ensure the implementation of that plan.

a2634.speaker: Report on ATF fund collections 2021-2023
a2634.speech: According to the report on funds collected in the AIDS Trust Fund for 2021-2023, collections increased from Sh1.06 billion in 2021 to Sh2.04 billion in 2023.

a2634.speaker: Jenister Mhagama, Tanzania Minister of Health
a2634.speech: Speaking by telephone with Mwananchi on Wednesday 22 January 2025 about how the Government has prepared following Trump’s decision: “This matter is being looked into but we are waiting to get complete information,” promising to give further clarification when she finished her meeting.

a2634.speaker: Dr Lilian Mwakyosi, Executive Director of the Dare organisation
a2634.speech: Said that because of the American President’s decision the challenge will be especially in essential needs, particularly the financing of health care for some medicines and treatment of vertical projects: “More than 90 percent of the resources relating to AIDS and HIV come from outside; PEPFAR contributes 40 percent and there are other organisations that contribute, including WHO, the United States Centers for Disease Control (CDC) and the Global Fund, and in all of these America puts in a lot of money, so you can see how we will be shaken” ; said Tanzania must prepare itself properly, and that although it has already begun putting strategies in place it has the capacity to contribute only six percent through the Ministry of Health budget and the AIDS Trust Fund (ATF).

a2634.speaker: Dr Lilian Mwakyosi, Executive Director of the Dare organisation
a2634.speech: Said there are services that will be directly affected by the current policies of America, including safe abortion and family planning projects: “The law says that if you receive funds you are required to do this and that, and what you are not required to do. With the current policies of America, there are some things we will have to stop doing, so we will act according to their requirements and not the needs of society” ; warned that there are groups that are helped to protect themselves, so the current policies will exclude them, and if there are no funds to look after those groups HIV infections may increase in the country.

a2634.speaker: Dr Elisha Osati, health consultant and expert
a2634.speech: Emphasised the importance of Tanzania investing in domestic resources in order to be self-reliant: “For HIV medicines and treatment we depend heavily on aid from America. The shaking of this aid should be a spur for us as a country to be more self-reliant in health and education” ; “The ATF fund is very important, but we have not used it properly. It is now time to put emphasis on this fund and to persuade other nations such as China to contribute more.”

a2634.speaker: Veronica Lyimo, Forum of Women Living with HIV
a2634.speech: Said that Trump’s argument aims to require countries that depend on aid to build sustainable systems of self-reliance.

a2634.speaker: Statistics (cited data)
a2634.speech: According to statistics, an HIV patient receiving antiretroviral medicines uses medicines worth 58.20 dollars per month; with more than 1.5 million patients in the country, the cost of medicines alone is more than Sh204 billion for a single month.

a2636.speaker: Dr Vamsi Krishna, managing director of Hetero Group of Companies
a2636.speech: “Hetero is pleased to partner with the Gates Foundation to create a pathway for the sustainable and affordable supply of lenacapavir.” He added that the collaboration aims to ensure access to innovative HIV medicines for patients in India and other low- and middle-income countries.

a2636.speaker: Trevor Mundel, president of global health at the Gates Foundation
a2636.speech: “Scientific advances like lenacapavir can help us end the HIV epidemic— if they are made accessible to people who can benefit from them the most.” ; “We are committed to ensuring that those at highest risk, who can least afford it, aren’t left behind.”

a2636.speaker: Public health experts
a2636.speech: See it as a transformative option for people who face barriers to daily oral PrEP, including stigma, adherence challenges and inconsistent access to medication.

a2636.speaker: Modelling / one study (cited)
a2636.speech: Modelling suggests that the introduction of lenacapavir has the potential to prevent significant numbers of HIV infections. One study showed that scaling up access to affordable lenacapavir to just four percent of the population in high-burden countries could prevent up to 20 percent of new infections.

a2784.speaker: Market watchers
a2784.speech: According to market watchers, amid the persistent liquidity constraints, the widening gap unveiled increased competition among banks to secure scarce foreign exchange, particularly the dollar.

a2784.speaker: Industry insiders
a2784.speech: Acknowledge that banks operate under substantial regulatory oversight, with the Central Bank closely monitoring rate adjustments to prevent volatility.

a2784.speaker: Analysts
a2784.speech: Some analysts speculate that such prolonged inertia could also signal internal policy rigidities or strategic choices designed to serve broader monetary policy objectives.

a2784.speaker: Analysts
a2784.speech: Analysts warn that sustained divergences could eventually expose deeper policy conflicts or market fragmentation, prompting either regulatory intervention or adjustments by banks to respond to imbalances.

a2934.speaker: Private security companies operating in Mali
a2934.speech: After nearly three decades of implementation, many support “a comprehensive revision of this legislative and regulatory framework in force” which, they say they observe, “does not take into account the major developments that have occurred in the sector, notably the emergence of cybercrime, asymmetric terrorism and cross-border attacks, and the rise of intelligent surveillance technologies”.

a2934.speaker: Ismaïla N. Diallo, promoter of the forum and expert in strategic security, intelligence and security governance in Mali
a2934.speech: Said the purpose of the forum was “to together make a lucid diagnosis, identify concrete levers for action and co-construct a shared vision of the role of private security in Mali” ; said the private security sector “mobilises thousands of young people and contributes to reducing unemployment and to strengthening the rule of law”, but stressed that it remains confronted with a lack of institutional support and suitable financing and a lack of dialogue between stakeholders ; believes it is becoming imperative to modernise the texts, strengthen control mechanisms and above all institutionalise a lasting collaboration between the public authorities and private companies: “In other words, we must transform complementarity into a factor of shared performance. This, in the service of national security.”

a2934.speaker: Representative of SAER Protect Mali, official sponsor of the forum
a2934.speech: Proposes “the adoption of a comprehensive, holistic and inclusive approach that takes into account all aspects of security” to meet the multiple security challenges Mali is going through.

a2934.speaker: Souleymane Diabaté, chief executive officer of Bridges Worldwide Security (BWS)
a2934.speech: Assured that support for the actors of the sector would not be lacking because “no sacrifice is too great for Mali”, he declared.

a3164.speaker: Vera Songwe, Executive Secretary of the UN Economic Commission for Africa (ECA)
a3164.speech: said that combatting bribery, money laundering and tax evasion should be a priority if Africa has to finance its transition to middle income status and increase prosperity.

a3164.speaker: Vera Songwe, Executive Secretary of the UN Economic Commission for Africa (ECA)
a3164.speech: called governments to take action on several fronts, and she insisted leadership was critical demonstrative effect important; as such governments should aggressively investigate and prosecute money launderers and companies that evade taxes.

a3164.speaker: Vera Songwe, Executive Secretary of the UN Economic Commission for Africa (ECA)
a3164.speech: "For a continent that needs substantial financial resources to meet its development needs, we should celebrate our accountability agencies, the auditor general, the chief justice and the media to support the collective effort" ; asked for more integrity and transparency among leaders and officials of the public and private institutions through asset declarations; and urged African countries to sign up to the international tax information treaties to enable exchange of information ; "Countries should also build human and technological capacities of agencies tasked with tackling Illicit financial flows, and institute information sharing and collaboration between relevant government agencies and ministries."

a3164.speaker: Vera Songwe, Executive Secretary of the UN Economic Commission for Africa (ECA)
a3164.speech: applauded countries that have ratified existing global and continental initiatives on halting Illicit financial flows.

a3164.speaker: Report of President Mbeki's high-level panel on illicit financial flow
a3164.speech: According to the report, the Continent loses between USD 50 billion and USD 80 billion a year due to illicit financial flows.

a3164.speaker: United Nations (estimates)
a3164.speech: UN estimates that the amount Africa loses through illicit financial flows is roughly double the Official Development Assistance that Africa receives, and also outweighs the USD 42 billion that the continent received in Foreign Direct Investment in 2017.

a3323.speaker: Economics Association of Malawi (Ecama) and the National Planning Commission (NPC) — joint final 2025/26 Budget Analysis Report
a3323.speech: Have observed that global indications point to donor funding uncertainty, yet Malawi’s development budget remains heavily dependent on donors; the analysis states that what compounds the situation is that the financial blueprint has been formulated in a fiscally challenging context of macroeconomic instability. “Recent global developments points to uncertainty around official development assistance for Malawi. For instance, the United States [US] Government recently issued a stay order on 28 January 2025, which led to the complete withdrawal of financial support by the United States Agency for International Development [USAid]. Similarly, the United Kingdom [UK] has announced plans to reduce aid spending from 0.5 percent to 0.3 percent of Gross National Income [GNI] beginning 2027. Statistics from the US Department of State show that USAid contributed an average of $350 million over the years, which is equivalent to 13.0 percent of the 2024/25 FY [fiscal year] budget.”

a3323.speaker: Economics Association of Malawi (Ecama) and the National Planning Commission (NPC) — joint 2025/26 Budget Analysis Report
a3323.speech: According to the analysis, funding gaps in the health sector are eventually going to undermine efforts to improve healthcare access, ultimately leading to failure in strengthening the health system and addressing other sub-sectors such as nutrition. “This is a worrisome development that requires urgent corrective action to ensure our aspiration of attaining a lower middle-income country by 2030 materialises. In terms of the alignment between the proposed 2025/26 budget and MIP-1, the analysis shows most of the focus areas within the pillars and enablers are underfunded or not financed altogether. This, however, may reflect prevailing economic, social and environmental realities to which the government is responding to, policy wise” ; the two institutions have tipped the government to be prudent in guarding resources allocated to the development budget, to accelerate implementation of transformational projects, to set up a multi-agency monitoring team to track expenditures in a timely manner, and to allocate more resources to large-scale farms.

a3323.speaker: World Bank (20th Malawi Economic Monitor)
a3323.speech: According to the World Bank’s 20th Malawi Economic Monitor, the mining sector could earn the country up to $43 billion in export earnings between now and 2040; according to the World Bank, proper management of mining resources revenue will be integral to the success of the sector and uplifting of the economy.

a3323.speaker: Simplex Chithyola Banda, Minister of Finance
a3323.speech: Told Parliament last week that the government has committed to ensuring that critical public services do not get adversely impacted following the US funding freeze; he cited the upward adjustment to the health sector as being one of the commitments of the government. “We have ensured that all affected critical services are provided for in the budget to ensure continued service delivery.”

a3341.speaker: Maureen Malave, Nutrition and Social Protection Lead at USAID Ghana
a3341.speech: Said the intervention was an important step in ensuring that communities not only have access to nutritious food but also good health and social services; indicated that livestock farming would be introduced with a focus on guinea fowls, roosters and rabbits as supplemental livelihood sources; said the farmers would be linked to grain dealers to ensure that excess grains can be transported to areas experiencing food shortage, thereby enhancing food security in the north. ; "The United States believes that support in times of crisis is not just about offering immediate relief, it is about building long-term resilience. By improving agricultural practices, diversifying livelihoods and improving the ability to respond to climate shocks, we can ensure vulnerable populations have access to the nutrition they need, the economic opportunities to thrive and the means to withstand future challenges."

a3341.speaker: Paulina Addy, Director of Women in Agricultural Development Directorate (WIAD), Ministry of Food and Agriculture
a3341.speech: Said the intervention would help victims of the dry spell build back better and boost food production; emphasised the need to adopt innovative solutions that would withstand the shocks of climate change and mitigate the impact on agriculture.

a3341.speaker: Shani Alhassan Shaibu, Northern Regional Minister
a3341.speech: Lauded the US government for the support and appealed to the awardees to use the funds strictly for the purposes for which the funds have been given. ; "Prudent and judicious use of the funds is required by the Government and the people of Ghana as well as the Government and People of the United States of America (USA). The program has its activities and expected outcomes, our focus should be on ensuring that at the end of the program period, the expected results and outcomes are achieved, and the evidence of those achievements should be there for all to see"; further entreated all the value chain actors of the programme to put in strategies and measures to ensure that gains made would be sustained to benefit future generations.

a3420.speaker: Zeng Yao, 1990s-born Pingyang local and pet-industry entrepreneur
a3420.speech: "Spend a weekend dressing up your dog for our pet fashion show. Browse our pet supply superstore. Tour the pet food factory right next door."

a3420.speaker: Zeng Yao, 1990s-born Pingyang local and pet-industry entrepreneur
a3420.speech: Explained that the real challenge lies in breaking into the market: "Historically reliant on exports, we've shifted focus to China's booming domestic market."

a3420.speaker: Zeng Yao, 1990s-born Pingyang local and pet-industry entrepreneur
a3420.speech: "This hybrid model blending livestream e-commerce, tourism, and retail drives brand visibility and cultivates influencers. Over 50 local pet brands now broadcast from the facility."

a3420.speaker: Zeng Yao, 1990s-born Pingyang local and pet-industry entrepreneur
a3420.speech: "This is a big business," said Zeng, who plans to replicate the Pet Town concept nationally, hoping more people will get to know Pingyang through its vibrant pet industry.

a3420.speaker: Chen Zhenbiao, resident of Shuitou township and founder of Peidi Animal Nutrition Technology Co., Ltd.
a3420.speech: Recalled: "In the 1990s, traders arrived seeking discarded pig and cow hides. None of us imagined those scraps would become premium pet chews!"

a3420.speaker: Tang Zhaobo, deputy general manager of Peidi
a3420.speech: "Consumers increasingly seek trusted brands and specialized products, creating a vast, segmented market."

a3420.speaker: Official from Pingyang county's culture, media, tourism and sports bureau (unnamed)
a3420.speech: "We're developing comprehensive pet-inclusive tourism: accredited boarding, pet-friendly campgrounds, dedicated buses, hotels, and self-service grooming stations. Our goal is to become a premier destination for pet lovers."

a3684.speaker: Nyesom Wike, Minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Nigeria
a3684.speech: Issued a bold charge to African leaders and investors to abandon the continent's longstanding reliance on foreign aid and take full responsibility for shaping its economic future; delivering the keynote address at the 2025 Innovate Africa Conference, insisted that Africa's development lies not in donor funding but in visionary leadership, home-grown investment, and renewed confidence in its people ; “Africa must now rise above aid, rediscover her strength, and rebuild her institutions. Development cannot be donated; it must be built. Our future must be crafted not in the conference rooms of donor agencies, but in the creative laboratories, farms, classrooms, and workshops of Africans determined to transform their continent.”

a3684.speaker: Nyesom Wike, Minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Nigeria
a3684.speech: On receiving the Innovate Africa Leadership Award 2025, dedicated the recognition to President Bola Ahmed Tinubu and the Nigerian people, saying it underscored Abuja's ongoing infrastructural renewal and governance reforms: “This honour belongs not to me alone, but to the resilient people of Nigeria, and especially to President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, whose bold vision for renewal has given me the platform to contribute to our nation's transformation.”

a3684.speaker: Nyesom Wike, Minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Nigeria
a3684.speech: Expressed concern that despite Africa's youth population and abundant natural wealth, progress remains stifled by weak institutions, unemployment, and failed governance systems: “How can a continent so richly blessed remain so constrained?” he questioned. “Leadership remains the fulcrum upon which the destinies of nations turn.” Called for a shift from transactional to transformational leadership, emphasizing humility, service, accountability, and difficult policy choices; praised President Tinubu's early reforms, especially fuel subsidy removal and decentralization efforts, as an example of leadership that “dares where others hesitate” ; “If we can reimagine leadership across Africa in this same spirit leadership that builds, not blames; that inspires, not divides then no mountain will be too high, and no dream too ambitious for our continent.”

a3684.speaker: Nyesom Wike, Minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Nigeria
a3684.speech: Highlighted that 70% of Africans are under 30, describing the demographic as “a revolution waiting to happen”: “The energy, creativity, and resilience of Africa's young population are not just assets; they are the very instruments of the continent's transformation,” he said, urging increased investment in education, digital literacy, innovation, and entrepreneurship; stressed that infrastructure must serve as an “equalizer,” connecting talent to opportunity and unlocking productivity on a continental scale.

a3684.speaker: Nyesom Wike, Minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Nigeria
a3684.speech: Referencing the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), noted that regional integration remains Africa's clearest path to prosperity: “The AfCFTA is a declaration of intent that Africa will no longer accept to be a supplier of raw materials and a dumping ground for finished goods. It is the cornerstone of Africa's second liberation the liberation of its economy.”

a3684.speaker: Nyesom Wike, Minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Nigeria
a3684.speech: Closing his remarks, challenged African leaders, investors, and citizens to stop waiting for external deliverance and assume full ownership of the continent's destiny: “History will not remember what we merely dreamed for Africa; it will remember what we did for Africa. The future will not be given to us. We must build it. And we must build it now.” Expressed hope that the ideas shared at the conference would inspire concrete steps toward making Africa “a land of fulfillment, dignity, and shared prosperity.”

a3684.speaker: Mazi Sam Ohuabunwa, Chairman of the occasion and former presidential aspirant
a3684.speech: Lamented that Africa continues to struggle under the weight of incompetent leadership and political systems designed to keep a few in power at the expense of national progress; warned that many political leaders in the continent attain leadership “by all means” and then build structures to perpetuate themselves or their families in government, rather than delivering development for citizens; said Africa must undergo what he called a “leadership metamorphosis” — a deliberate transformation that will unlock the continent's economic potential, strengthen competitiveness, and accelerate sustainable development; said such a shift will drive economic growth, improve living standards, and attract long-term investment that is not tied to election cycles or foreign dictates.

a3684.speaker: Mazi Sam Ohuabunwa, Chairman of the occasion and former presidential aspirant
a3684.speech: Urged leaders to adopt Africa-led solutions, embrace inclusive and sustainable growth, and promote inter-country cooperation that breaks down outdated boundaries; stressed the need for political systems that allow every citizen including the youth and those with “silent talent” to participate meaningfully in national development; emphasized that Africa must shift “from aid to partnerships” that genuinely serve the continent's interests; listed key leadership competencies required for Africa's transformation, including sound and digital education, innovation capacity, effective communication, emotional intelligence, integrity, accountability, and the ability to translate ideas into action ; “Leadership is not for bullies or daydreamers. We need leaders who can make sacrifices, keep their promises, and deliver results in the national interest not personal gain.”

a3817.speaker: Richard Werner, economist known for his theory of credit creation
a3817.speech: argues that banks are not intermediaries that lend out deposits, as commonly believed; instead, banks create money through the process of credit creation – when a bank issues a loan, it simultaneously creates a deposit in the borrower’s account, effectively generating new money.

a3817.speaker: Reserve Bank of Malawi
a3817.speech: According to the Reserve Bank of Malawi, only about 30% of Malawians have access to formal banking services.

a3817.speaker: World Bank data
a3817.speech: According to World Bank data, countries like Germany and France have over 30 commercial bank branches per 100,000 adults, while Malawi lags far behind.

a4047.speaker: Claver Gatete, Executive Secretary of the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (UNECA)
a4047.speech: said more than 20 African countries are either already facing debt distress or on the brink ; said in 2024, Africa's total public debt shot up to US$1.86 trillion, with average debt-to-GDP ratios rising from 44.4% in 2015 to 66.7% today ; "When debt repayments outweigh investments in health and education combined, we must question the sustainability and human cost of our fiscal path." ; "Africa is not merely confronting a debt crisis; it is facing a development crisis – one where debt servicing competes directly with health, education, infrastructure and the fundamental right to development."

a4047.speaker: Claver Gatete, Executive Secretary of the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (UNECA)
a4047.speech: said across Africa, access to concessional finance is narrowing, while tariff escalations are weakening market access for African goods ; said many African countries are facing higher borrowing costs, reduced export revenues and tighter budgets, at a time when fiscal expansion is essential for inclusive growth ; said the cost of capital has surged.

a4047.speaker: Claver Gatete, Executive Secretary of the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (UNECA)
a4047.speech: said the international financial lifelines Africa once relied on, including Official Development Assistance, are fading; today, 83 percent of USAID programmes have been cancelled and traditional partners are tightening their budgets.

a4047.speaker: Claver Gatete, Executive Secretary of the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (UNECA)
a4047.speech: said the G20 Common Framework, unfortunately, remains slow, opaque and creditor-biased.

a4074.speaker: Dr. Luke Bawo, Executive Director of the Liberia Medicines and Health Products Regulatory Authority (LMHRA)
a4074.speech: Has outlined progress made by his organization during the past five months; said though significant strides have been made in safeguarding public health in Liberia, he acknowledged that challenges still remain ; noted at the MICAT regular press briefing that the organization has been active in seven counties and is focusing on the waste management of health products ; said the LMHRA has undergone staff restructuring to enhance operational efficiency and has made strides in de-escalating tensions within the organization to foster a culture of inclusiveness ; disclosed that regulatory frameworks surrounding narcotics and psychotropic substances have been effectively migrated from the Ministry of Health to the LMHRA, reinforcing its authority in this sector ; mentioned significant achievements, including the formation of a reappointed Hearing Board designed to offer impartial reviews of alleged violations in health product regulations.

a4074.speaker: Liberia Medicines and Health Products Regulatory Authority (LMHRA) press release
a4074.speech: Quotes Dr. Bawo as indicating that the construction of a new laboratory is underway, which is vital for the organization's capacity to effectively assess and regulate health products, and as stating that an assessment has started in Maryland County to establish the LMHRA's Region-4 office, demonstrating the regulatory authority's commitment to decentralization and increased coverage.

a4074.speaker: Dr. Luke Bawo, Executive Director of the Liberia Medicines and Health Products Regulatory Authority (LMHRA)
a4074.speech: Did not shy away from discussing the challenges facing the LMHRA, particularly highlighting issues such as system clogs due to expired products in circulation that pose risks to public health; the rising issue of street peddling of medicines; the lack of adherence to donation regulations, leading to inefficiencies within the supply chain; and the need for laboratory system strengthening and enhanced technological support to manage regulations effectively.

a4074.speaker: Dr. Luke Bawo, Executive Director of the Liberia Medicines and Health Products Regulatory Authority (LMHRA)
a4074.speech: Says his organization remains optimistic, emphasizing the need for collaborative efforts of key stakeholders such as the Ministry of Health, WHO, USAID, and other partners in striving to achieve WHO maturity level 3 and ISO 17025 accreditation for LMHRA's laboratory.

a4267.speaker: President of the Republic of Ghana
a4267.speech: Pronouncements that he was placing his presidency on the line, marshalling the security forces as the commander in chief of the armed forces, did not deter the players of the galamsey supply chain.

a4312.speaker: US government
a4312.speech: Approved last Thursday an “emergency humanitarian waiver” that authorizes the immediate resumption of mother-to-child HIV treatment and prevention services, after the revocation of the US executive order announcing the suspension of foreign development assistance for ninety days to assess programmatic efficiency and alignment with the US government’s foreign policy.

a4312.speaker: US State Department (note)
a4312.speech: According to a note from the US State Department, the measure is supported by the US President’s Emergency Plan for HIV/AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) – the largest global initiative to respond to the disease.

a4331.speaker: Felix Amenounve, Director General of the Regional Securities Exchange (BRVM)
a4331.speech: "Out of 30 SMEs supported, not one is yet listed."

a4331.speaker: Felix Amenounve, Director General of the Regional Securities Exchange (BRVM)
a4331.speech: "Africa must encourage the birth of its giants in the classroom."

a4331.speaker: Abdoulaye Bio Tchane, Benin's Minister of State in charge of Planning
a4331.speech: Insisted on the responsibility of States: "the State cannot be the main provider of jobs" - it must instead guarantee macroeconomic stability, improve infrastructure (in particular access to electricity and the internet), and simplify the lives of entrepreneurs ; stressed that "more than 90% of companies in Benin are SMEs, but too few scale up."

a4331.speaker: Speakers at the opening of the Africa SME Champions Forum
a4331.speech: Agreed on an unsparing assessment: despite the efforts made in recent years, African SMEs still struggle to access financing, innovation, and the scale needed for their durability.

a4415.speaker: Humanitarian NGOs (figures)
a4415.speech: According to the figures of humanitarian NGOs, more than 5.4 million people are in a precarious food situation and 2.8 million children suffer from acute malnutrition in the Sahel.

a4415.speaker: “Elles du Sahel” network
a4415.speech: Organised a round table on 28 May 2025 to present the recommendations from the previous year’s meetings, whose main demand is the need to increase funding to face the challenges of the Sahel ; reiterated its urgent appeal to the international community to guarantee the active participation of women and girls in the efforts for peace, security and development in the Sahel.

a4415.speaker: Report “Listen to the voices of the Sahel” (“écoutez les voix du Sahel”), “Elles du Sahel” network
a4415.speech: Synthesising the main recommendations, it was presented to international donors in Brussels, highlighting the urgency of maintaining investment in favour of women and girls, notably in strategic sectors such as education, health and gender justice.

a4415.speaker: Maïmouna Dioncounda Dembélé, founding member of “Elles du Sahel”
a4415.speech: Said that in a context of prolonged crisis, women’s organisations, civil society and states must invest in crucial areas, beyond questions of security and defence ; “Today, we must invest more in health and education, sectors that are often neglected, notably as regards gender-specific issues. One of our major recommendations is to increase funding for gender issues, in a Sahel weakened by terrorism,” insisting on the need for transnational responses to transnational challenges.

a4483.speaker: Major General Assoumane Abdou Harouna, Governor of the Niamey Region
a4483.speech: On the security situation: "Since 26 July 2023, the Niamey Region has seen a very appreciable improvement in its security situation. The general state of our administrative entity is stable, under absolute control and marked by restored order and discipline thanks to the CNSP's directives. We have waged a relentless offensive against petty banditry and deployed robust strategies to counter terrorist threats... We created the morals brigade and reactivated the sanitary police... Every day, 21 vehicles of the CRS patrol the five communes. In the first half of 2025, the Niamey City Police carried out 3,545 patrols, 1,294 crackdown operations and 59 raids, arresting more than 12,000 people... Niamey [is] a dazzling showcase of Niger: a cleaner, safer city where the population can live and work in complete peace of mind, with the certainty that the State watches over it with unshakeable vigilance."

a4483.speaker: Major General Assoumane Abdou Harouna, Governor of the Niamey Region
a4483.speech: On changes in the population's daily life and state of mind: "The two years under the CNSP have profoundly transformed the daily life of Niamey's inhabitants and their perception of our nation's progress. These changes have strengthened discipline, sharpened collective consciousness and revived patriotism... A relentless fight is being waged against prostitution, drug and shisha consumption, and delinquency in urban and school settings... Support for the current leadership is manifest, because the population perceives a tangible improvement in security and an affirmed will for national sovereignty. The inferiority complex has been swept away; the West is no longer an absolute reference. Our people have realised that they can count on their own genius to transform the country... A new type of citizen has been born, whose compasses are patriotism, love and the defence of the homeland."

a4483.speaker: Major General Assoumane Abdou Harouna, Governor of the Niamey Region
a4483.speech: On the Grand Irrigation Programme (PGI): "The Grand Irrigation Programme (PGI) is a major strategic vision for our food sovereignty and our economic independence... We have rehabilitated 320 hectares in Niamey: 54 hectares at Goudel, 64 hectares at Lamorde, 96 hectares at Kirkissoye, and 106 hectares at Saguia Amont. These actions drastically reduce our rice imports and strengthen our food security... The PGI aims to reduce our dependence on rice imports from more than 83% to only 10-15% by 2027, with a total of more than 39,700 hectares to be developed or rehabilitated... ONAHA's record is eloquent: the rehabilitation of Saguia Amont for more than one billion CFA francs, the mobilisation of jobs, and a total production of 13,844.67 tonnes of paddy rice on 2,667.235 hectares farmed by nearly 3,000 farmers. Our strategy is bearing fruit; sovereignty is under construction."

a4483.speaker: Major General Assoumane Abdou Harouna, Governor of the Niamey Region
a4483.speech: On the population's challenges and hopes: "The main challenge remains the persistence of security threats... On the socio-economic front, Niger remains confronted with poverty. Despite projections of agricultural growth, extreme poverty remains a reality. International sanctions have had a harmful impact on our economy, hampering humanitarian aid. Strong demographic growth poses considerable challenges in terms of access to basic services, employment and resources... Environmental challenges, such as recurrent flooding, are also a major concern... One of the major hopes is the consolidation of our national sovereignty... The Grand Irrigation Programme embodies an immense hope for food self-sufficiency and economic development... The population of Niamey navigates between persistent challenges and growing hopes, fuelled by the quest for sovereignty, the advances of the PGI, a more aware youth and an improving urban environment."

a4676.speaker: Ashem Songwe, MP for Likoma Island
a4676.speech: “We have seen the President’s commitment to infrastructure development, particularly in the road sector. However, Likoma Island and other water-dependent areas need attention. I would like to ask you, Your Excellency, what the government intends to do to modernise our water transportation and port infrastructure.”

a4676.speaker: Mike Bango, MP for Kasungu North
a4676.speech: “Our nation’s forex woes are largely due to insufficient exports. I would like to ask you, Mr President, if you are satisfied with the performance of our diplomats as marketers of Malawi. Why are foreigners succeeding where our diplomats are failing?”

a4676.speaker: Paul Dumembe Nkhoma, MP for Kasungu North East
a4676.speech: Is expected to ask Chakwera about the government’s strategies to combat inflation and address food insufficiency.

a4676.speaker: Salim Bagus, MP for Chikwawa Central
a4676.speech: “The recurring floods have devastated these areas. I would like to ask you, Mr President, if the government has immediate plans to purchase land in upland areas to relocate these vulnerable populations.”

a4676.speaker: Kenneth Ndovie, MP for Karonga Nyungwe
a4676.speech: Will seek updates on the Chitipa-Nyika-Rumphi Road and the rehabilitation of the Mpata Road ; “With the President’s five-year term nearing its end, we need clarity on these projects.
