The completion of the Ilomba Road and other outstanding roads in the Northern Region is also vital for our development.”

a4676.speaker: George Chaponda, Leader of the Opposition
a4676.speech: Refused to send questions to the President, saying his Sona was not truthful and therefore he could not send questions to receive untruthful answers.

a4730.speaker: Osman Saleh, Eritrea's Foreign Minister
a4730.speech: Delivered a briefing to diplomats and UN officials in Asmara, addressing the recent flood of misinformation and false accusations being peddled against Eritrea ; categorically rejected false claims of Eritrean troops presence in the Tigray Region of Ethiopia, reaffirming that the EDF units have been fully redeployed within the country's internationally recognized borders since November 2022 ; dismissed attempts to scapegoat Eritrea for Ethiopia's ongoing internal crises, clarifying that Eritrea views the Pretoria Agreement as an internal Ethiopian matter and has no intention of intervening in the ongoing power struggle in Tigray ; criticized Ethiopia's dangerous rhetoric regarding access to the Red Sea.

a4730.speaker: John Foster Dulles, in a September 1952 speech to the UN Security Council
a4730.speech: "From the point of justice, the opinions of the Eritrean people must receive consideration. Nevertheless, the strategic interest of the United States in the Red Sea basin and considerations of security and world peace make it necessary that the country be linked with our ally, Ethiopia."

a4730.speaker: Permanent Peoples' Tribunal of the International League for the Rights and Liberation of People (foreword to the 1980 Proceedings)
a4730.speech: "No important struggle - be it in terms of military intensity or in terms of political impact - is so poorly known, indeed ignored, as is that which the Eritrean people have been engaged in for 20 years."

a4730.speaker: International Commission of Jurists
a4730.speech: Stated that "Of all the people who, since the Second World War, have been the victims of Great Power rivalries and ambitions, perhaps the one with the greatest claim for consideration is the people of Eritrea. Nevertheless, no nation has yet been willing to raise the issue of the rights of these people in the United Nations. The truth is that the 'Eritrean question' is a source of embarrassment both to the UN itself and to almost all 'interested parties'."

a4730.speaker: Isaias Afwerki, Eritrean President (address to the UN General Assembly, 1993)
a4730.speech: "[The years of] deafening silence pained our people. It also gave a free hand to the aggressors, thereby prolonging our suffering and increasing the sacrifices we had to make. But it neither shook our resolve nor undermined our belief in the justness of our cause and the inevitability of our victory. As an Eritrean proverb says: 'The rod of truth may become thinner but it cannot be broken.' Indeed, justice has finally prevailed. This is a source of hope and happiness not only for the Eritrean people, but for all those who cherish justice and peace."

a4796.speaker: Leaders of the Nigerian oil and gas industry (2025 NOG Conference sessions)
a4796.speech: Lauded the contributions of NCDMB and highlighted the impact the Nigerian Oil and Gas Industry Content Development (NOGICD) Act has made in transforming the oil and gas landscape. They emphasised the need for continued support by Government and other stakeholders.

a4796.speaker: Green Energy International Limited (GEIL)
a4796.speech: Praised NCDMB for enabling the commissioning of the Otakikpo Crude Export Terminal in Rivers State, Nigeria’s first indigenous onshore crude oil export terminal in over 50 years.

a4796.speaker: Felix Omatsola Ogbe, NCDMB Executive Secretary
a4796.speech: Highlighted NCDMB’s “Nigeria First” policy during the conference’s opening, underscoring a commitment to prioritising local goods, services, and capabilities across the oil and gas value chain, building on the NOGICD Act of 2010 and President Bola Tinubu’s Executive Orders, with the policy mandating local procurement unless foreign alternatives are justified, aiming to retain economic value, create jobs, and drive technological innovation.

a4796.speaker: Abdulrazaq Isa, Chairman of the Independent Petroleum Producers Group (IPPG)
a4796.speech: Highlighted that indigenous producers now account for over half of the nation’s oil and gas output, and that the divestment and transfer of onshore and shallow water assets from international oil companies to local operators has enabled IPPG members to target 1.3 million barrels per day of oil and 4.5 billion cubic feet of gas by 2027.

a4796.speaker: Bashir Bayo Ojulari, Group CEO of NNPC Ltd
a4796.speech: Highlighted NCDMB’s support for the Ajaokuta-Kaduna-Kano (AKK) Gas Pipeline’s progress, including its successful crossing of the River Niger, with completion expected by Q4 2025.

a4796.speaker: Industry leaders at the NOG Conference
a4796.speech: Defended NCDMB’s local content framework against criticisms that it inflates costs, arguing that its economic benefits, including job creation and GDP growth, far outweigh short-term expenses.

a4796.speaker: Dr Daere Akobo, Pana Holdings
a4796.speech: Highlighted NCDMB’s role in projects like Africa’s first digital refinery, emphasizing technology’s role in enhancing efficiency.

a4796.speaker: George Onafowokan, Coleman Cables and Wires
a4796.speech: Praised NCDMB’s data-driven approach, noting a 56% local content achievement as a significant milestone.

a4796.speaker: Dr Ernest Nwapa, pioneer Executive Secretary of NCDMB
a4796.speech: Noted that over 16 African nations have adopted similar local content laws, inspired by Nigeria’s NOGICD Act.

a4796.speaker: Nasir Alfa Mohamed, Ghana’s Deputy Chief Executive
a4796.speech: Called for standardized regulations and joint regulatory bodies to enhance cross-border collaboration.

a4796.speaker: Farouk Ahmed, NMDPRA
a4796.speech: Emphasized the PIA’s Midstream and Downstream Gas Infrastructure Fund as a model for de-risking investments.

a4796.speaker: Panelists at NOG Energy Week
a4796.speech: Stressed the need for sustained investment in human capital to support Nigeria’s refining ambitions, as infrastructure alone is insufficient without skilled professionals. ; Argued that fragmented data and operational inefficiencies, not local content mandates, are the primary cost drivers.

a4796.speaker: Anibor Kragha, ARDA
a4796.speech: Highlighted Nigeria’s $2 billion expenditure on imported petrochemicals in 2023 as a gap that local capacity development could address.

a4803.speaker: Elijah Ngurare, Namibian Prime Minister
a4803.speech: Said the situation of Angolan kids as young as four years old on the streets is a case the government regards as urgent.

a4803.speaker: Lucia Witbooi, Vice President
a4803.speech: Called on Lüderitz councillors and community members to collectively address challenges facing the local disability centre during her visit.

a4803.speaker: Suzan Ndjaleka, Deputy Minister of Health and Social Services
a4803.speech: Has called for teamwork and unity from the health staff to improve Namibians’ access to health care and social services.

a4803.speaker: Members of Parliament (MPs)
a4803.speech: Raised various concerns regarding the budget allocation towards the Ministry of Health and Social Services, and gave their suggestions on where they expect to see improvement in the sector and how it could be better capacitated to cater to all citizens nationwide.

a4803.speaker: Ministry of Health and Social Services (Namibia)
a4803.speech: Has reaffirmed that it is making rehabilitation and assistive technology services available across the country; currently such services are offered free of charge only at seven hospitals.

a4803.speaker: Kalumbi Shangula, Health and Social Services Minister
a4803.speech: Says the ability to see and the gift of vision are two of the most essential aspects of human health and well-being.

a4803.speaker: Dr. Kalumbi Shangula, Minister of Health and Social Services
a4803.speech: Has responded to concerns raised by Popular Democratic Movement (PDM) MP Winnie Moongo about the shortage of cardiotocography papers at Windhoek Central Hospital.

a4803.speaker: Winnie Moongo, Popular Democratic Movement (PDM) MP
a4803.speech: Raised concerns about the shortage of cardiotocography papers at Windhoek Central Hospital.

a4859.speaker: Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) economic report for the fourth quarter of 2024
a4859.speech: According to the report, total foreign exchange (FX) inflows into the Nigerian economy rose by 21% quarter-on-quarter, reaching $27.8 billion; FX outflows increased by 31% q/q to $10.4 billion, leaving a net FX inflow of $17.4 billion for Q4 '24; inflows from autonomous sources surged by 48% q/q to $16.3 billion while inflows through the CBN declined by 4% q/q to $11.5 billion; net external reserves climbed to $23.1 billion by the end of 2024 from $4.0 billion in 2023, and gross external reserves increased by $6 billion to $40.19 billion; Nigeria posted a Balance of Payments surplus of $6.83 billion in 2024.

a4859.speaker: Analysts at FBNQuest (analyst note shared with Daily Independent)
a4859.speech: Projected that the momentum would carry into the first quarter of 2025, contingent on the continuation of the CBN's proactive measures aimed at improving FX liquidity and investor confidence: "We anticipate the trend of positive inflows to continue in Q1 '25 driven by CBN's actions and initiatives to boost market liquidity," the analysts said ; expect the trend to persist driven by continued CBN initiatives such as unifying exchange rates, managing inflation, and encouraging foreign portfolio investment, but also cautioned that net FX inflows may taper slightly due to a seasonal rise in FX outflows through the CBN, primarily tied to the repayment of external debt obligations, which typically peak in the first quarter.

a4859.speaker: Hakama Sidi-Ali, CBN's Acting Director of Corporate Communications (statement)
a4859.speech: Attributed the positive balance to comprehensive reforms, enhanced data accuracy, and improved trade and financial account performance: "The current and capital account recorded a combined surplus of $17.22 billion, underpinned by a strong goods trade surplus of $13.17 billion."

a4859.speaker: Hakama Sidi-Ali, CBN's Acting Director of Corporate Communications
a4859.speech: Said the 79.5% reduction in net errors and omissions, to negative $5.10 billion from negative $24.90 billion in 2023, demonstrates significant improvement in data capture and reporting frameworks, aligning with international standards and increasing investor trust.

a4859.speaker: CBN Governor
a4859.speech: Emphasized that the overall BoP surplus signals the success of Nigeria's structural reforms: "The positive turnaround in our external finances is evidence of effective policy implementation and our unwavering commitment to macroeconomic stability" ; "This surplus marks an important step forward for Nigeria's economy, benefiting investors, businesses, and everyday Nigerians alike."

a4920.speaker: Insecurity Insight (report, March 2025)
a4920.speech: Reports that the freeze on USAID funding ordered by President Donald Trump on 20 January 2025 provoked a massive rejection of foreign aid on social media in the Sahel; the study reveals a sharp rise in criticism of NGOs and international donors in Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger, fuelled by nationalist and pro-Russian rhetoric; rejection of aid is particularly strong in Burkina Faso (645 negative comments out of 810) and Mali (587 out of 698), while Niger shows more mixed sentiment (44 out of 96); criticisms concern economic dependency, suspicions of corruption and Western influence perceived as interference; stresses that the online rejection of humanitarian aid has had real-world repercussions, with the expulsion of NGOs such as Acted and Action pour le Bien-Être (APBE) in Niger, and that the repression of pro-aid voices through insults and accusations of treason on social media contributes to restricting humanitarian space.

a4920.speaker: Malian social media commenter (anonymous, cited in the study)
a4920.speech: “Development aid has not developed any country, it only serves donors to exert their pressure.”

a4920.speaker: Malian social media user (anonymous, cited in the study)
a4920.speech: “The West gives us aid with conditions and blackmail. Russia, for its part, respects our sovereignty!”

a4920.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a4920.speech: Criticised “unnecessary spending” on development aid and demanded that American aid directly benefit the strategic interests of the United States.

a4995.speaker: Donald Porusingazi, political analyst
a4995.speech: "Side events are akin to a cattle-fattening project as they take place on the ground and will never replace the need for thorough continental preparations that should have taken place on African soil ahead of this conference." ; Warned that "Without a unified front, Africa risks being sidelined in negotiations that will shape the future of global finance" ; He said the "fragmentation dilutes bargaining power and undermines the continent's ability to secure structural reforms."

a5176.speaker: Cyriaque Edouard Dossa, magistrate and doctor of law (presenter at the FONAC/USAID seminar on transnational crime and gender)
a5176.speech: Presented the theme “Transnational organised crime: what implications for human rights and the development of a nation?” and set the scene with tangible realities: “In these places you will find vehicles and above all vehicle parts that in principle can only be obtained on order from the parent company. But, given that these accessories are often the fruit of theft in the country, as is also often the case abroad... These parts are often the product of armed robbery, of loss of human life, of loss of property rights, of the right to free movement, which are nothing other than human rights.” He also observed that in African legislative and presidential elections “candidates spend billions of our francs without seeking to know the origin of the said funds, which for the most part are laundered capital. Having come to power, experience seems to prove that their first reflexes are not along the lines of development but of satisfying their benefactors, an attitude that dangerously compromises the future of nations.”

a5176.speaker: Cyriaque Edouard Dossa, magistrate and doctor of law
a5176.speech: Observed that the opening of borders, the free movement of capital and goods and the development of telecommunications also reveal the use of the various channels of globalisation for criminal ends, and noted that the lack of regulation of economic and financial activities at the international level gives criminal phenomena, once confined to a single territory, immeasurable possibilities of expansion.

a5176.speaker: Cyriaque Edouard Dossa, magistrate and doctor of law
a5176.speech: Said the term “Organised Cross-border Crime” is not an offence but should be understood as “a lodge, a consortium, a federation of offences whose list is not exhaustive”, and explained that “the United Nations Convention against Transnational Organised Crime retains a few of them, including money laundering and corruption, supported by many mechanisms for successful repression such as international cooperation for the purposes of confiscation, extradition, transfer of sentenced persons, and mutual legal assistance.” He added that “the expression ‘organised crime’ was born in the United States in the 1920s... during the Prohibition period... of which the most famous figure is that of Al Capone.”

a5176.speaker: Maurice Cusson (cited)
a5176.speech: Holds that “by organised crime is generally meant a structured and hierarchical association of professional criminals obeying binding rules and methodically planning the illicit enterprises they monopolise through the systematic use of violence.”

a5176.speaker: Raymond Gassin (cited)
a5176.speech: Considers that “organised crime means crime whose preparation and execution are characterised by methodical organisation and which, most often, provides its perpetrators with their means of existence.”

a5176.speaker: Michel Quille (cited)
a5176.speech: Aligns himself with the definition adopted in the United States in 1967 during the preparatory work for the Crime Control Act of 1970: “Organised crime is a society that seeks to carry on its activities outside the control of the citizens and their government. Its action is not improvised but results from very complex conspiracies woven over many years and intended to procure control of a complete field of activity with a view to accumulating as much profit as possible.”

a5176.speaker: Raphael Parizot (cited)
a5176.speech: Analyses that “organised crime is a modern form of delinquency that is difficult to pin down.”

a5176.speaker: Gilles Favarel-Garrigues, researcher (cited)
a5176.speech: Wonders whether transnational organised crime is not a concept to be buried, because of the difficulty of defining its contours.

a5176.speaker: United Nations Convention against Transnational Organised Crime of December 2000 (Palermo Convention)
a5176.speech: States that the expression “organised criminal group means a structured group of three or more persons existing for a period of time and acting in concert with the aim of committing one or more serious crimes or offences established in accordance with the present Convention, in order to obtain, directly or indirectly, a financial or other material benefit”; and that “serious crime means conduct constituting an offence punishable by a maximum deprivation of liberty of at least four years or a more serious penalty.”

a5176.speaker: Cyriaque Edouard Dossa, magistrate and doctor of law
a5176.speech: Stated that transnational organised crime encompasses practically all serious criminal activities motivated by profit that have an international character, listing drug trafficking, arms trafficking, human trafficking, clandestine migration, financial and economic delinquency, cybercrime, corruption, fraud and tax evasion, money laundering, hostage-taking, maritime piracy and terrorism as the most frequent in West Africa; and noted that cybercrime's most profitable field for criminals is identity theft, which generates about 1 billion dollars each year.

a5176.speaker: Experts on transnational organised crime (cited by the magistrate)
a5176.speech: Estimate that between 30 and 40 tonnes of cocaine from South America transit through West Africa each year.

a5176.speaker: UNODC
a5176.speech: Discovered between 2009 and 2012 drug factories, notably of methamphetamine, in Guinea-Bissau, Guinea-Conakry and Nigeria.

a5176.speaker: United Nations mission (mid-1990s)
a5176.speech: Estimated that eight million small arms and light weapons must be in free circulation in West Africa, outside the control of states.

a5176.speaker: NATO
a5176.speech: Reported the disappearance of at least 10,000 missiles that could constitute a mortal danger both for Libya's neighbouring countries and for the regions frequented by terrorists, notably the Sahel-Sahara and the Horn of Africa.

a5176.speaker: International Labour Organisation (ILO)
a5176.speech: Estimated, at a recent time, that the number of trafficking victims was, at any given moment, about 2.4 million, with profits of about 32 billion dollars.

a5176.speaker: Cyriaque Edouard Dossa, magistrate and doctor of law
a5176.speech: On the means of combat: said the international community has always made the fight against transnational organised crime a major challenge, and listed the instruments adopted — the UN Convention against Transnational Organised Crime of December 2000, the UN Convention against Corruption, the UN Convention of 15 December 1997 for the Suppression of Terrorist Bombings, Security Council resolutions on terrorism, African Union, ECOWAS and UEMOA texts, and the African Centre for Studies and Research on Terrorism (CAERT) in Algiers — and underlined that several West African states have for the past dozen years adopted domestic legal texts against transnational organised crime.

a5202.speaker: July Moyo, Zimbabwean Minister of Energy and Power Development
a5202.speech: Made the call for member states to urgently adopt collaborative and innovative strategies to tackle the growing energy and water insecurity that threatens economic growth and social development across the region, underscoring the critical need for regional integration and accelerated infrastructure development to meet rising demand and climate-related pressures: “Energy and water are the lifelines of our communities, economies and ecosystems. Insecurity in either will undermine production, weaken economic resilience and hinder growth.” ; Said that over 172 million people in SADC remain without access to electricity and only 40 percent of the population has adequate sanitation, and that compounded by population growth, urbanization, aging infrastructure, vandalism, and underinvestment, both energy and water sectors are under strain.

a5202.speaker: July Moyo, Zimbabwean Minister of Energy and Power Development
a5202.speech: “In Zimbabwe alone, we lose approximately US$4 million annually to transformer theft and related damage. These criminal acts disrupt both power and water supply and demand a regional crackdown through tougher laws, technology deployment, and community awareness.”

a5202.speaker: July Moyo, Zimbabwean Minister of Energy and Power Development
a5202.speech: Said that although Zimbabwe's installed generation capacity stands at nearly 3 000 MW, only 1 200–1 600 MW is currently achievable, far short of peak demand estimated at 2 000 MW, a situation which has led to periodic load shedding and increased reliance on imports.

a5202.speaker: July Moyo, Zimbabwean Minister of Energy and Power Development
a5202.speech: Noted progress in renewable energy deployment, saying Zimbabwe is ramping up solar and hydro investments, including projects backed by pension funds such as the 25 MW Centragrid Nyabira Solar PV Park and the upcoming 100 MW Munyati Solar Plant: “We have developed our National Energy Compact with a goal to install 1.2 million solar home systems and solarize 35 000 villages by 2030 under the Presidential Rural Development Program.”

a5202.speaker: July Moyo, Zimbabwean Minister of Energy and Power Development
a5202.speech: Called for urgent completion of interconnection projects to allow all SADC mainland countries, particularly Angola, Malawi and Tanzania, to join the Southern African Power Pool (SAPP), thus enabling greater electricity trade and improved grid stability ; urged member states to capitalise on solar potential, particularly in countries like Botswana, Namibia, Zimbabwe, and South Africa, and called for increased regional manufacturing and market creation for clean energy technologies.

a5202.speaker: July Moyo, Zimbabwean Minister of Energy and Power Development
a5202.speech: Warned that El Niño-induced droughts, pollution, and underutilised irrigation are undermining access and sustainability, as currently only 71 percent of the region's population has access to safe drinking water: “This is a serious indictment. We must scale up water infrastructure investment and prioritize sanitation resilience, particularly as climate impacts worsen.”

a5202.speaker: July Moyo, Zimbabwean Minister of Energy and Power Development
a5202.speech: Applauded countries like Tanzania for rapidly increasing electricity access, connecting 8 million people in two years, and encouraged member states to share best practices and scale up investments.

a5202.speaker: July Moyo, Zimbabwean Minister of Energy and Power Development
a5202.speech: “If we don't act decisively now, the SADC Industrialization Strategy and Roadmap will remain a pipe dream. Let this meeting be a turning point for the region. We must move from plans to action.”

a5464.speaker: Anita Kiki Gbeho, UN humanitarian coordinator for South Sudan
a5464.speech: Warned that an estimated 9.3 million people are expected to face humanitarian crisis in 2025, a figure slightly higher than the 9 million people projected for this year; lauded humanitarian organizations for relentless efforts to support the needy population; said 4.2 million people have been reached with humanitarian intervention in 2024, through food distribution, shelter and camp management among others ; "The 2024 Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan was about 64% funded. As a result, we were able to reach 4.2 million women, men, boys and girls with different forms of critical assistance, including food, nutrition, health, water and sanitation, camp coordination, camp management, education, shelter, non-food items and protection services." ; "According to the 2025 Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan, 9.3 million people, 70% of the population, will require some form of humanitarian assistance in 2025. Of these, the humanitarian community will target 5.4 million with an appeal for 1.7 billion dollars."

a5464.speaker: Albino Akol Atak, Minister for Humanitarian Affairs and Disaster Management
a5464.speech: Attributed the successful humanitarian response this year to high collaboration and coordination and called for continuous strengthening of collaboration to achieve the targeted 5.4 million people in the 2025 humanitarian needs and response: "We managed to respond to the needs of people in this year, 2024, simply because there was high collaboration and coordination. So the same thing next year, if we want to respond to this target number 5.4 million people. We need to strengthen and to increase that collaboration." ; He assured partners and humanitarian organizations of his government's continued cooperation: "The government expressed its sincere appreciation for solidarity and support provided by humanitarian donors and partners over the past years and looks forward to continuing cooperation to respond to the most active needs of vulnerable people in South Sudan."

a5601.speaker: U.S. Embassy in Lilongwe
a5601.speech: Has indicated it needs more time to assess the orders' potential impact.

a5601.speaker: Milward Tobias, economist
a5601.speech: Points out that Malawi's position in U.S. priorities post-review remains unclear, leaving the nation vulnerable to funding cuts.

a5696.speaker: Netumbo Nandi Ndaitwah, Vice President of Namibia
a5696.speech: says the government will relay support to ensure that the project succeeds ; "Therefore, our government stands firm behind initiatives like the Harambe-Oyetu project. Recognising their pivotal role in food security and job creation through agriculture. Yes, this project, no doubt, though it's now in the hands of the National Youth Council, at its initial stage should still require the support of multiple stakeholders. Of course, our Ministry of Agriculture or the government, through the Ministry of Agriculture, should also continue to give technical support in terms of giving or allowing extension service officers."

a5696.speaker: Netumbo Nandi Ndaitwah, Vice President of Namibia
a5696.speech: further stressed the need for regional inhabitants to buy locally fresh produce for project continuity and warned that it would not turn into a white elephant.

a5696.speaker: Marius Sheya, Kunene Governor
a5696.speech: Giving the project overview, said similar projects will be set up in all the constituencies, with plans to also expand the Harambe-Oyetu project to incorporate fish and chicken farming ; "When I went to the Roots Project in Stampriet, I said to myself, We will also do something similar in Outjo, in Opuwo in Khorixas, in Kamanjab, and in Okanguati. We will do something similar, and this is just a replica."

a5696.speaker: Zhao Weiping, Chinese Ambassador to Namibia
a5696.speech: said they sponsored the project because of the China-Namibia Corporation's interest in agricultural development ; "I know great efforts are being made by the Namibian government to improve the nation's agricultural sector. As a friend of Namibia, China has always taken what Namibia needs as our priority in implementing development assistance projects in Namibia. Since agriculture is so important to Namibia, we are certainly determined to do more in this area."

a5696.speaker: Dr. Felix Musukubili, National Youth Service Commissioner and project custodian
a5696.speech: promised the garden would be cultivated to become the bread basket of the town and region.

a5911.speaker: Desalegn Abebaw, CEO of the Ethiopian Deposit Insurance Fund (EDIF)
a5911.speech: “The required funding will be substantial.” ; On the backup deal with the Ministry of Finance allowing the Fund to draw on the Treasury when a failure’s liabilities exceed premiums already paid: “Agreements have already been concluded.”

a5911.speaker: National Bank of Ethiopia (NBE) stability report
a5911.speech: Warned that if the 10 biggest depositors at each bank pulled their money at once, 20 of the 29 banks would breach liquidity rules ; Singled out “deposit concentration” as a pressing danger.

a5911.speaker: Merga Wakeya, Operations Manager of the EDIF
a5911.speech: “We've a shortage of funds to increase the coverage. We need to collect enough funds.”

a5911.speaker: Merga Wakeya, Operations Manager of the EDIF
a5911.speech: On levying premiums on foreign banks and shifting toward risk-based pricing: “It has to be done cautiously. Lenders may protest.” ; “It's to be done cautiously,” Merga told Fortune, repeating the mantra that reform should not shock the system it wants to protect ; Hopes the upcoming capital market will offer new investment vehicles and perhaps allow the Fund to place longer-dated paper for higher returns without sacrificing liquidity.

a5911.speaker: Tefera Tesfaye (PhD), chief executive of Africa Village Microfinance
a5911.speech: “It affects our liquidity” ; “There’s been no response yet from regulators to pleas for relief. A microfinance institution must start with solid lending funds and sufficient resources at hand.”

a5911.speaker: Desalegn Abebaw, CEO of the Ethiopian Deposit Insurance Fund (EDIF)
a5911.speech: Disclosed to Fortune on the shelved automated payout system: “Our budget was capped at 35 million Br. But the final assessment put the figure at 72 million Br; the cost far exceeded our expectations.” ; Called Treasury bills “a key income source” that helps stabilise the balance sheet ; “We're latecomers,” noting Ethiopia is the 148th country to adopt deposit insurance.

a5911.speaker: Tilahun Girma, veteran consultant
a5911.speech: Argued for diversification into high-yield fixed deposit products to hedge inflation and floated reinsurance with foreign insurers to spread risk: “A robust financial sector safety-net is crucial for a healthy financial system.” ; Warned that new threats shadow lenders, pegging cyberrisk exposure at 1.3 billion Br and saying loose management of credit concentrations could push banks “toward insolvency” if left unchecked ; “The National Bank should adopt a flexible approach, tailoring premiums based on an institution’s maturity and exposure in the financial market.”

a5911.speaker: IMF (study)
a5911.speech: According to an IMF study, strong onsite and offsite monitoring — “the eyes and ears” of a healthy safety net — can spot trouble early.

a5911.speaker: Ethiopian Deposit Insurance Fund (EDIF)
a5911.speech: Says it needs scale, and plans to raise premiums once it completes work on a risk-weighted schedule under which institutions with weaker capital buffers or higher non-performing loans would pay up.

a6128.speaker: Kananelo Khalla, 30, Lesotho man living with HIV since birth and former Youth Ambassador for the Elizabeth Glaser Paediatric Aids Foundation (EGPAF)
a6128.speech: “I disclosed my status to her... after each check-up, I explained everything to her, my viral load was undetectable, so we protected ourselves properly.” ; “Today, we have Prevention of Mother-To-Child Transmission (PMTCT) programme. It’s easier now to protect children from HIV infection.” ; “The health services were different back then.” ; “Parents weren’t taking proper steps to protect their children. So, I kept getting sick until I was tested at Baylor in 2007, and it was revealed that I had been living with HIV.”

a6128.speaker: Kananelo Khalla, 30, Lesotho man living with HIV since birth
a6128.speech: Reflected on his childhood: “The journey wasn’t easy.” ; “I faced stigma from other children. My cheeks would bruise, and I didn’t have the energy to play. I was teased a lot. As a child, I didn’t understand the care I needed, and I couldn’t even explain what was wrong.” ; “I kept getting sick until I tested HIV-positive at Baylor Clinic in 2007. When I first began treatment, I was treated for both TB and HIV, a co-infection.” ; “But when I started attending sessions at Baylor and met other children living with HIV, I started understanding my condition. We were taught how to take care of ourselves. Still, it wasn’t easy, I had to skip school often to take TB treatment.” ; “Sometimes she couldn’t afford transport, and I walked. Some organisations chipped in when needed. It was tough. Organisations visited me at school and home, and other children wondered why. I made up stories, saying I was an orphan receiving help.”

a6128.speaker: Kananelo Khalla, 30, Lesotho man living with HIV since birth
a6128.speech: “It makes me proud that my child is HIV-free.” ; “It shows that HIV can stop with me – it doesn’t have to be passed down to future generations.” ; “Between my son and me, the difference is huge. I used to visit clinics three to five times a month. He only needs to go once every few months.”

a6128.speaker: Kananelo Khalla, 30, Lesotho man living with HIV since birth
a6128.speech: Directed his words to US President Donald Trump regarding the January 2025 cuts to foreign aid: “HIV should not be politicised. We were close to ending it. I would ask him to reconsider and restore funding for a future free of HIV.”

a6128.speaker: Kananelo Khalla, former Youth Ambassador for the Elizabeth Glaser Paediatric Aids Foundation (EGPAF) in Lesotho
a6128.speech: “I supported young people because I understood their struggles. I helped them stay on treatment and believe in themselves,” expressing fear that without support, adherence to medication among youth will decline; “Infections will rise,” he warned, recalling that without proper support young people often struggle to adhere to treatment, causing their viral loads to soar; fears that without solid HIV/Aids funding from countries like the US, there are risks that HIV will become generational again: “Without psychosocial, emotional, and spiritual support, people may default and co-infections will rise. Treatment access will drop.”

a6128.speaker: Mangose Sithole, PMTCT Programme Manager, Lesotho Ministry of Health
a6128.speech: Noted that in 2013 and 2017, Lesotho made it mandatory for all HIV-positive pregnant and breastfeeding women to begin lifelong antiretroviral treatment immediately after diagnosis – a major step toward eliminating paediatric HIV.

a6128.speaker: ‘Masebeo Koto, Lesotho Ministry of Health
a6128.speech: “We are at 94 percent with our pregnant women, which means we still need to work even harder,” said during the August 5, 2025, meeting. Added: “We can see that because of the PMTCT program, we are now seeing the infections going down because of the programme.”

a6128.speaker: US Foreign Assistance website (data)
a6128.speech: According to it, Lesotho received a total of $1,663,866,392 in US funding between 2001 and 2025, with HIV/Aids among the top-funded sectors at $73.61 million; the website indicated it was last updated on August 22, 2025.

a6128.speaker: US Embassy in Maseru
a6128.speech: On September 5, 2025, reported that the $6 million initial funding provided in July 2025 will continue supporting lifesaving HIV care and treatment services in the four districts of Maseru, Mohale’s Hoek, Mafeteng and Thaba-Tseka – leaving six other districts, including Mokhotlong, Botha-Bothe, Leribe, Berea, Quthing and Qacha’s Nek, without the same level of support.

a6128.speaker: Study published in April 2025 by the Society for Science and Education
a6128.speech: Noted that USAID’s relief budget accounts for 43 percent of global humanitarian financing: “Its unexpected reduction represents serious implications for the global health sector, threatening lives of millions, like those in Tanzania, eSwatini, and Lesotho, where the USAID provided HIV treatment and support to more than 350 000 people (Global Health Council, 2025). Without USAID assistance, these people are defenceless against HIV.”

a6171.speaker: US Agency for International Development (USAID), correspondence seen by APA
a6171.speech: Justified the termination of the grants by “reasons of convenience” and “the interest of the American government”, in accordance with a directive of US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, acting administrator of USAID ; ordered the beneficiaries to immediately halt all activities linked to the funding and to inform their partners and subcontractors ; also ordered other USAID-supported health programmes, although not directly linked to HIV, to cease their activities.

a6171.speaker: Marco Rubio, US Secretary of State and acting administrator of USAID (directive)
a6171.speech: Issued the directive in accordance with which the South African PEPFAR grants were terminated.

a6199.speaker: Axel Cramer, Napha (Namibia Professional Hunting Association) president
a6199.speech: According to Cramer, both hunting expos were a tremendous success, with Namibia’s flag flying high in the US. "About 30 Namibian exhibitors participated in Nashville from Wednesday to Saturday. Some of our Napha members confirmed there was significant interest, particularly in big-game hunting trips for elephants, crocodiles and buffaloes, but not as much for plains game," Cramer told Network Media Hub (NMH) from Nashville ; he added that there was strong competition from Africa at the expos, particularly from South Africa, Tanzania and Zambia.

a6218.speaker: Ismaïl Omar Guelleh, President of the Republic of Djibouti
a6218.speech: In a declaration from the summit rostrum, vigorously condemned “the permanent aggression of the Zionist regime against the Palestinian people in general, and particularly in the Gaza Strip, with its daily widening of the zone of genocide and ethnic cleansing” ; “This includes the deliberate and growing targeting of shelters, schools, hospitals, … levelling them to the ground,” he denounced, stressing how much “the brotherly Palestinian people is undergoing a liquidation of its existence in Gaza as well as a systemic denial of its land in the occupied West Bank.”

a6218.speaker: Ismaïl Omar Guelleh, President of the Republic of Djibouti
a6218.speech: Expressed his “categorical rejection of the attacks against innocent civilians in Gaza, including mass killings and barbaric bombardments” ; “Gaza is enduring a new tragedy; its inhabitants, more than two million, are taken hostage by the Zionist occupation, which mistreats them, forces them to flee, deprives them of water, food and medicine,” the Djiboutian President protested, saying that in the face of the gravity of the situation the Arab and Muslim world must act quickly and “do everything to put an end to the merciless aggression of the State of Israel against the brotherly people of Palestine.”

a6218.speaker: Ismaïl Omar Guelleh, President of the Republic of Djibouti
a6218.speech: Elevated to the rank of an imperative duty incumbent on the Arab and Muslim world the need “to call collectively on the international community to assume its legal and ethical responsibilities” and to “oppose attempts to liquidate the Palestinian cause by working with the defenders of peace in the world to reinvigorate a just and lasting solution to the conflict in the Middle East, which can only be achieved by ending the Zionist occupation of the land of Palestine, with East Jerusalem as capital.”

a6218.speaker: Joint extraordinary summit of the League of Arab States and the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (resolutions)
a6218.speech: Adopted a series of resolutions through which the assembled Arab and Muslim leaders notably: reaffirmed the centrality of the Palestinian cause and their support, by all means, for the Palestinian people in its resistance to liberate its occupied territories; stressed the impossibility of regional peace in the Middle East in the absence of a settlement of the Palestinian question, holding Israel responsible for the persistence and aggravation of the conflict; warned against the consequences of Israel’s vengeful aggression in the Gaza Strip, the West Bank and the city of Al Quds Al-Sharif; refused to characterise the war waged by Israel as legitimate self-defence or to justify it on any pretext, and consequently called for breaking the blockade, imposing humanitarian aid convoys and calling on countries to stop exporting arms and munitions to the occupation authorities; asked the Security Council to adopt a resolution condemning Israel for the barbaric destruction of the hospitals of the Gaza Strip and its ban on the delivery of medicine, food and fuel; and urged the Prosecutor General of the International Criminal Court (ICC) to complete the investigations into war crimes and crimes against humanity against the Palestinian people and to support the legal and political initiatives of the State of Palestine.

a6243.speaker: Dr (Mrs) Kemi Ogunyemi, Special Adviser to the Governor of Lagos State on Health
a6243.speech: In her keynote address, described the initiative as a landmark step toward the realisation of the Babajide Sanwo-Olu administration’s THEMES+ agenda, particularly in delivering timely and quality emergency healthcare to Lagosians: “These new ambulance points represent not just infrastructure, but hope and access to lifesaving care” ; noted that the structures were strategically placed in Agege, Agbowa, Masha (Surulere), Badagry, Mile 2, Epe, Shomolu, Igando, Iba and Ibeju-Lekki to ensure broader and faster emergency medical coverage: “By locating ambulances closer to the people, we can significantly cut down on the time it takes to get medical help in critical situations” ; “We are not just launching facilities today, we are reinforcing our promise to save lives, support frontline responders, and build a healthier, safer Lagos for all.”

a6243.speaker: Dr (Mrs) Kemi Ogunyemi, Special Adviser to the Governor of Lagos State on Health
a6243.speech: Praised the collaborative spirit that brought the project to fruition, singling out the contractor, Mr Sulaiman Hammed, for what she called “professional dedication beyond contractual obligations”, and acknowledged Mr Moshood Akintayo, a beneficiary of LASAMBUS services, for voluntarily beautifying the Agege ambulance point with his personal resources.

a6243.speaker: Dr Olusegun Ogboye, Permanent Secretary, Lagos State Ministry of Health
a6243.speech: In his welcome remarks, shared his deep personal passion for emergency services and highlighted LASAMBUS as a cause he has championed throughout his tenure: “This is not just another ribbon-cutting ceremony. It’s a signpost of progress, a culmination of years of planning and passionate work” ; explained that the ten new points are part of a larger blueprint to upgrade and establish more strategically located points on the roads, ambulance bases in hospitals, forward-operating posts in local government areas, and trauma centres across Lagos, citing already functional trauma centres in Epe and Tollgate and ongoing works at MCC Eti-Osa: “We’re building more than structures; we’re building systems. From infrastructure to communication upgrades, every piece fit into a larger vision of seamless, responsive emergency medical service delivery.”

a6243.speaker: Dr Olusegun Ogboye, Permanent Secretary, Lagos State Ministry of Health
a6243.speech: Commended the LASAMBUS team for their dedication and resilience, noting that the addition of new points will naturally increase their workload: “Even as we celebrate today, we acknowledge the increased demands on our responders. Your sacrifice doesn’t go unnoticed” ; recognised the contributions of the community, citing Mr Moshood Akintayo’s gesture as “the highest form of civic partnership any government agency could ask for”, and urged others to emulate such community ownership of public assets.

a6243.speaker: Sulaiman Hammed, MD/CEO of Hamibra Integrated Nigeria Ltd
a6243.speech: Presented a project brief explaining the evolution of the prefabricated model from earlier versions that were vulnerable to environmental damage and unrest: “This new model is fortified, mobile, and designed to stand for over 50 years” ; revealed that the structure includes an ambulance personnel station equipped with executive furniture, anti-burglar German steel panels and hybrid plasma cooling for staff comfort, and that the ambulance hangar is reinforced with top-grade steel; said the modular structures are not only transferable but also cost-effective in the long term, and expressed gratitude to Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu for supporting innovation and to the Special Adviser and Permanent Secretary for their leadership and trust in local contractors.

a6243.speaker: Mrs Rasheedat Saka, Deputy Director of Nursing, representing LASAMBUS
a6243.speech: Applauded the commissioning as a game-changer for pre-hospital care delivery: “These new points drastically improve our comfort, readiness, and response times. So with this in place, we are ready to respond come sun or rain” ; appreciated the Ministry for responding to the needs of ambulance personnel, citing training and continuous capacity-building efforts; reminded Lagosians of the availability of emergency toll-free numbers 767 and 112, urging citizens to call either number during emergencies.

a6243.speaker: Mr Moshood Akintayo, beneficiary of LASAMBUS intervention
a6243.speech: Recalled how the service saved his life during an accident earlier this year: “They showed up fast, treated me on-site, and transported me to the hospital, all at no cost” ; “This is my small way of giving back. LASAMBUS gave me a second chance at life.”

a6272.speaker: ActionAid Nigeria
a6272.speech: Has joined the global community in marking World Humanitarian Day, under the theme “Strengthening global solidarity and empowering local communities,” meant to honour the courage of humanitarian workers everywhere, including those who have lost their lives in the line of duty.

a6272.speaker: Andrew Mamedu, Country Director of ActionAid Nigeria (press statement)
a6272.speech: “They were friends and colleagues who showed bravery, and their sacrifice must never be forgotten. Today is also a moment to reflect on the urgency of strengthening solidarity with the millions of people across Nigeria whose lives are disrupted by conflict, disaster, disease, and inequality.”

a6272.speaker: Andrew Mamedu, Country Director of ActionAid Nigeria (press statement)
a6272.speech: “The year 2025 has laid bare the enormity of humanitarian challenges facing our nation. From the escalating violence in Benue, Zamfara, and Borno that has left families displaced and grieving, to the catastrophic floods in Mokwa, Rivers, Adamawa, and Lagos that have washed away homes and livelihoods, the scale of suffering is staggering.” ; “In Benue State alone, more than half a million people have been uprooted, surviving in overcrowded conditions with limited food, water, or health care. Across the northeast, the insurgency continues to threaten lives and undermine stability, while in the northwest, banditry and mass abductions have torn families apart. At the same time, Nigeria is battling a devastating hunger crisis, with nearly 31 million people facing food insecurity and thousands of children dying of malnutrition in Katsina and other states.” ; “The humanitarian crisis has been further compounded by outbreaks of preventable disease. Cholera has resurfaced across several states, fuelled by flooding and poor sanitation. Lassa fever, meningitis, diphtheria, and dengue fever in Edo have stretched already fragile health systems to breaking point. Each of these shocks highlight how quickly a health risk can escalate into a full-blown humanitarian emergency when poverty, conflict, and climate change converge.”

a6272.speaker: Andrew Mamedu, Country Director of ActionAid Nigeria (press statement)
a6272.speech: “The Federal and state governments, private sector, and international partners should urgently address the funding gap. Governments must scale up domestic humanitarian financing. The Nigerian private sector should increase support for crisis affected communities. The private sector to move beyond corporate social responsibility tokenism and play a transformative role in building resilience. This includes prioritising investments in food assistance, nutrition, health care, education, and climate resilience for crisis-affected regions. Nigerian businesses, private foundations philanthropists, and financial institutions should leverage their resources and innovation to fill critical gaps in humanitarian response, while also partnering directly with local organisations who understand community realities.” ; “International partners must prioritise flexible, long-term resources that go directly to local organisations to ensure that the withdrawal and cut of foreign aids does not deepen the suffering of millions.”

a6272.speaker: Andrew Mamedu, Country Director of ActionAid Nigeria (press statement)
a6272.speech: “ActionAid Nigeria believes that responding to these multiple crises cannot be business as usual. Communities are not passive recipients of aid, they are leaders, organisers, and agents of change, and they must be recognised as such. Women and young people have always been the first responders in moments of crisis, yet their leadership remains underfunded and undervalued. We therefore urge: The Federal Government, state governments, and local authorities to put crisis-affected communities, especially women and youth at the centre of humanitarian planning and response. This means not only consulting communities but ensuring they have decision-making power, flexible funding, and resources to lead their own responses. Governments should create enabling policies and budget lines that sustain women-led and youth-led initiatives, recognising that these groups are often the first to act and the most trusted in times of crisis.” ; “ActionAid Nigeria calls for urgent investment in local humanitarian leadership, particularly, women-led and youth-led responses, that have proven to be both effective and transformative.”

a6322.speaker: Obert Jiri, Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Lands, Agriculture, Fisheries, and Rural Development
a6322.speech: Said Zimbabwe can tap into the growing global meat market, which is expected to reach $1.3 trillion by 2027, by adding value and enhancing exports: "With the global meat market expected to reach $1.3 trillion by 2027, there lies a significant opportunity for countries like Zimbabwe to enhance exports and value addition. By addressing these critical areas, we can develop a resilient livestock sector that strengthens food security, fosters economic resilience, and moves us closer to achieving Vision 2030, wherein livestock plays a pivotal role in our nation's development." ; urged farmers to commit to actionable solutions that will evolve the livestock sector into a sustainable, inclusive, and globally competitive industry ; said livestock is not merely an economic asset but a cornerstone of rural livelihoods, food security, and cultural identity.

a6322.speaker: Obert Jiri, Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Lands, Agriculture, Fisheries, and Rural Development
a6322.speech: "To boost the livestock sector, the Ministry in 2021 launched the Livestock Growth Plan (LGP), an implementation tool of the Agriculture Food Systems and Rural Transformation Strategy (AFSRTS)." ; "The LGP seeks to establish a $2 billion livestock economy by 2025, anchored on the following pillars: animal health, nutrition, and genetics. The plan addresses long-standing challenges in the livestock subsector, such as tsetse infestation, foot-and-mouth disease, tick-borne diseases, and dip tank rehabilitation and construction." ; emphasized that the full implementation of the plan would restore Zimbabwe's status as a regional livestock powerhouse.

a6322.speaker: Obert Jiri, Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Lands, Agriculture, Fisheries, and Rural Development
a6322.speech: Said, in light of the El Niño-induced drought, that his Ministry is implementing robust drought mitigation strategies, including the establishment of 1 620 Drought Mitigation Ward Centres (DMWC) and supporting the construction of water troughs for 10 000 Village Business Units (VBUs): "The government launched a blitz borehole drilling program aimed at providing water for both humans and livestock across the country. We are also supporting mass vaccination and deworming of livestock to enhance their chances of surviving the drought period." ; "In collaboration with development partners, we have implemented feed intervention strategies, providing vital support such as hay, silage, and beef survival meal for livestock sustenance. Our targeted feed supplementation focuses on vulnerable districts, particularly within Matabeleland, distributing 9 665 metric tons out of 15 000 metric tons of maize silage and 280 metric tons out of 600 metric tons of wheat silage to distressed wards." ; said these interventions have saved two million cattle at high risk of death due to the drought.

a6322.speaker: Obert Jiri, Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Lands, Agriculture, Fisheries, and Rural Development
a6322.speech: Highlighted that access to financial resources remains a significant obstacle for many farmers, stressing that financing growth within the livestock sector is fundamental to realizing its full potential.

a6580.speaker: Eyob Tekaleign (PhD), State Minister for Finance
a6580.speech: Declared early last week, standing before members of the international community while briefing them on the new "homegrown" economic reform agenda, that the foreign exchange crunch should stop defining the Ethiopian economy.

a6580.speaker: Eyob Tekaleign (PhD), State Minister for Finance
a6580.speech: Acknowledged the successes of the statist policy, which brought impressive growth in GDP and per capita income as well as expansion in infrastructure and social services in health and education, driven by public investments financed through the mobilisation of domestic savings and prioritisation of credits ; "[However], the economic progress has not been entirely successful in inspiring structural transformation." He accepted the challenges that come along in the form of inflationary pressure, a massive trade deficit, a chronic shortage of foreign currency and increasing unemployment ; said foreign currency shortages have become one of the defining binding constraints to businesses as a result of the persistent current account deficit ; "Rapid increases in external debt in the context of poor project executions and export performance led to a high risk of debt distress."

a6580.speaker: Eyob Tekaleign (PhD), State Minister for Finance
a6580.speech: "The capacity building of the implementing institutions is one of the critical areas spotted in the reform." ; "Creating a focus of efficiency on the institutions by restructuring them to build capacity is one of the focus areas of the reform plan."

a6580.speaker: Abiy Ahmed (PhD), Prime Minister of Ethiopia
a6580.speech: "The Reform Agenda is our pro-job, pro-growth, and pro-inclusivity pathway to prosperity." ; "Join us on this path." ; "Acknowledging that the next chapter of Ethiopia's growth and development requires a more active private sector, we opened up key economic activities to private investment." ; "We moved the needle further than many had anticipated, and we continue to push further with renewed vigour and enthusiasm." ; praised the team that designed the plan as "Ethiopia's finest minds" ; said he hopes the reform agenda will "propel Ethiopia into becoming the African icon of prosperity" by 2030 ; "The reform agenda is close to my heart."

a6580.speaker: Members of the international community (audience at the briefing)
a6580.speech: Were receptive to the "ambitious" reform the administration of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed rolled out and agreed it is "doable".

a6580.speaker: Zemedeneh Negatu, consultant and board/global chairman of Fairfax Global
a6580.speech: Noted that one good thing about the tabled plan is recognising past achievements and capitalising on them ; "It's built on the successes of the last 15 years," Zemedeneh told Fortune.

a6580.speaker: Zemedeneh Negatu, consultant and board/global chairman of Fairfax Global
a6580.speech: Sees urbanisation as also overlooked as one of the components, which should have been accorded higher priority: "Since urbanisation is occurring rapidly across the country, giving focus to it early on would help to achieve growth and prosperity," he told Fortune.

a6580.speaker: Members of the Development Assistance Group (DAG)
a6580.speech: Hailed Eyob's admission of what ails the economy as "candid."

a6580.speaker: Mamo Mihretu, senior policy advisor to the Prime Minister
a6580.speech: Said the reform agenda was designed in response to these constraints, as well as the inefficiencies in the economy.

a6580.speaker: Eyob Tesfaye (PhD), macroeconomist
a6580.speech: Views the reform plan as remarkable, profound and excellent in terms of forethought, and believes most of the reform areas had already been forwarded to policymakers as recommendations over the past couple of years, showing the government has begun to listen: "This is a major departure from the past." ; "The commitment is huge." ; said what differentiates the current plan from previous ones is its emphasis on supply-side reform: "The programme seems to focus on enhancing the efficiency gain." ; "It also keeps macroeconomic stability at the core." ; said implementation of the reforms will require significant external financing on top of domestic savings and privatisation proceeds: "The additional external financing is expected to be mobilised from multilateral and bilateral development partners in the form of concessional and de-risked financing."

a6580.speaker: Eyob Tesfaye (PhD), macroeconomist
a6580.speech: Fears that the challenge will come while bringing the plan down to earth, and that lack of institutional strength could be one of the obstacles manifested during implementation, as many institutions have no previous experience in addressing economic problems comprehensively.

a6580.speaker: Vera Songwe (PhD), Executive Director of the Economic Commission for Africa
a6580.speech: Narrowed down the cost to realise the reform agenda to 10 billion dollars, of which 60pc is new foreign direct investment and the remainder to bring down Ethiopia's external debt exposure ; advises that if Ethiopia wants to follow in the footsteps of countries such as China, Laos and Vietnam it should achieve a ratio of domestic savings mobilisation against GDP of 20pc, from its current 11pc.

a6747.speaker: Samuel Torbi, cocoa farmer and chair of the Assin Fosu branch of the Cocoa, Coffee and Sheanut Farmers Association (COCOSHE)
a6747.speech: On climate-smart farming practices learned through COCOBOD and GIZ training: "This keeps moisture in and weeds out. It also feeds the soil. You'll see plenty of worms and millipedes here. That's how you know the land is alive." ; "We now use compost instead of chemicals. Our yields are better, and the cocoa is safer."

a6747.speaker: Samuel Torbi, cocoa farmer and chair of the Assin Fosu branch of COCOSHE
a6747.speech: On farmers' inability to afford chocolate: "Some of us have never even seen a bar of chocolate. We grow the cocoa, but we can't afford the products made from it." ; "To buy a single bar, you might need GHC70 to GHC100... Most farmers just can't afford that. We produce the cocoa, but it is the town folks who eat the chocolate." ; "At COCOBOD offices, they drink Milo and snack on Pebbles. But when they visit us farmers, they never think to bring any. And yet, it's our beans they use."

a6747.speaker: Samuel Torbi, cocoa farmer and chair of the Assin Fosu branch of COCOSHE
a6747.speech: On the nutritional benefits farmers are denied: "If it truly makes people healthier, why are we the ones left out? Are our bodies and minds less important?"

a6747.speaker: Samuel Torbi, cocoa farmer and chair of the Assin Fosu branch of COCOSHE
a6747.speech: On inclusion and fairness: told this reporter that cocoa farmers aren't looking for handouts - "We want fairness. If Ghana is making chocolate from our cocoa, then COCOBOD and the companies must ensure that some of it reach the people who grow the beans. Let our children taste what we produce. Let us feel part of the story." ; "It's not just about chocolate. It's about dignity." ; "Let the people who grow cocoa be part of Ghana's chocolate story. Let justice be as sweet as the chocolate we produce."

a6747.speaker: Farouk Quansah Nyame, Senior Manager at the Cocoa Marketing Company
a6747.speech: Admitted that local consumption of cocoa remains low and, in a media briefing, emphasized that COCOBOD's Public Affairs Department is stepping up its campaign to make cocoa a regular part of Ghanaian diets: "Cocoa is good for health. More Ghanaians need to benefit from what we produce."

a6796.speaker: Enyinnaya Abaribe, Chairperson of the Senate Committee on Power
a6796.speech: Identified outdated and inadequate infrastructure as the primary cause of recurring power failures.

a6796.speaker: Haeagwoo Lee and Sangwoo Park, BK Energy representatives
a6796.speech: Proposed a mini-grid system modelled after South Korea's energy framework.

a6796.speaker: Haeagwoo Lee, BK Energy representative
a6796.speech: Said South Korea, with a population of about 50 million, generates 130,000 megawatts without relying solely on a centralised national grid.

a6796.speaker: Adeola Olamilekan, chairman of the committee on appropriations
a6796.speech: Sponsored the amendments adjusting the 2025 budget, which resulted in the reallocation of funds to Recurrent (Non-Debt) Expenditure increased from N13 trillion to N13.5 trillion, an addition of N500 billion, and Capital Expenditure reduced from N23.9 trillion to N23.4 trillion.

a6796.speaker: Godswill Akpabio, Senate President
a6796.speech: Announced during plenary the summons of National Security Adviser Nuhu Ribadu, National Intelligence Agency Director-General Mohammed Mohammed, and State Security Services Director-General Oluwatosin Ajayi over allegations that USAID had provided financial support to global terrorist groups, including Boko Haram; said the security chiefs would appear in a closed-door session to verify the claims.

a6796.speaker: Ali Ndume, senator representing Borno South Senatorial District
a6796.speech: Sponsored the motion to summon the security chiefs over the allegations that USAID had provided financial support to global terrorist groups, including Boko Haram.

a6796.speaker: The Senate (resolution)
a6796.speech: Urged the federal government to honour the late Ijaw leader, Edwin Clark, by naming a national monument after him in recognition of his contributions to Nigeria's unity and development; observed a minute silence in Mr Clark's honour and resolved to send an official delegation to his burial ceremony.

a6796.speaker: Joel Onowakpo (Delta South) and South-south senators
a6796.speech: Moved the motion urging the federal government to honour the late Edwin Clark.

a6796.speaker: Sani Musa, Chairperson of the Senate Committee on Finance
a6796.speech: Announced at a press briefing in Abuja a two-day public hearing on the controversial tax reform bills proposed by President Bola Tinubu, to take place on Monday, 24 February, and Tuesday, 25 February; confirmed that key officials and stakeholders have been invited to contribute to the proposed reforms.

a6796.speaker: Natasha Akpoti-Uduaghan, Kogi Central Senator (PDP)
a6796.speech: Protested against the relocation of her seat within the chamber and insisted on retaining her original seat, thereby challenging Senate rules that require senators to occupy designated seats to be recognised when speaking.

a6912.speaker: Airbus and AviaDev joint study
a6912.speech: Revealed that Ethiopian Airlines can eye an opportunity to grow and expand by introducing nonstop flights on unserved or underserved routes, identifying 11 routes that previously had nonstop flights and uncovering five intra-continental and 10 international underserved routes involving Africa ; noted "Ethiopian Airlines, with its strategic positioning and modern fleet, could potentially fill this gap, providing a much-needed direct connection and enhancing its footprint in the intercontinental travel market" ; urged that introducing direct flights on high-potential intra-African routes including Abuja-Nairobi and Cape Town-Lagos would enhance travel convenience, reduce journey times, and stimulate new demand ; found the Mumbai-Johannesburg route to be the second most underserved market and projected captured traffic in 2026 that could sustain six directional flights a week using a widebody aircraft in the 250-seater category.

a6912.speaker: Airbus report
a6912.speech: Acknowledges that geopolitical issues, air service agreements, and airport slot constraints can impact route serviceability.

a6912.speaker: Airbus study
a6912.speech: Noted "The modernity of its fleet stresses the Airline's commitment to operational efficiency, passenger comfort, and environmental sustainability through reduced emissions and improved fuel efficiency" ; showed the benefits of incorporating new destinations into an established hub-and-spoke network, using nonstop flying services to generate additional traffic and revenue ; said Ethiopian Airlines' ability to stimulate traffic and capture market share through competitive services shows its potential to operate on other unserved or underserved routes successfully.

a6912.speaker: Mesfin Tassew, CEO of Ethiopian Airlines
a6912.speech: Believes that a dedicated department at the Ethiopian Airlines Group explores new routes, considering factors such as passenger traffic, demand, and profitability: "There're certainly underserved routes in Africa," he said. "But our desire isn't the only factor determining our entry."

a6912.speaker: Mesfin Tassew, CEO of Ethiopian Airlines
a6912.speech: Recalled instances where securing air traffic rights took a long time or was outright denied by civil aviation authorities in some African countries, even after attempting to cater to underserved routes, and pointed to ongoing efforts to increase flights from Nigeria and Kenya, yet approvals from authorities in these countries are still pending.

a6912.speaker: Mesfin Tassew, CEO of Ethiopian Airlines
a6912.speech: "Fifth freedom is not our priority," he told Fortune, referring to the right to carry passengers from a foreign country to another, while en route to/from a home country.

a6912.speaker: Mesfin Tassew, CEO of Ethiopian Airlines
a6912.speech: Confirmed Ethiopian Airlines' plans to start five new destinations in the fiscal year and that the Airline will continue relying on its hub-and-spoke model, hoping for wider adoption of SAATM principles ; "Increasing air transport will bring a multitude of benefits for African countries."

a6912.speaker: Mesfin Tassew, CEO of Ethiopian Airlines
a6912.speech: Said Ethiopian Airlines is open to partnerships with existing airlines or establishing new ones, citing collaborations in Zambia, Malawi, and Togo, but acknowledged setbacks, such as the suspended project in Nigeria following a political transition and delays in launching a joint venture in the DR Congo announced two years ago.

a6912.speaker: International Air Transport Association (IATA) latest annual report
a6912.speech: Reveals that Africa contributes only two percent to the number of worldwide passengers despite accounting for nearly a fifth of the global population.

a6912.speaker: Ahmed Kellow, former CEO of Ethiopian Airlines
a6912.speech: Recalled that Ethiopian Airlines was an early entrant into intracontinental air travel, primarily operating East-West routes, but has yet to establish sufficient flight paths to North African countries like Morocco or Algeria: "What works for one carrier may not work for the other," he said, noting that it took eight years for Ethiopian flights to China to become profitable ; believes that the Airline's professional staff, reputation for safety, and financial resources can help it outcompete smaller carriers for greater market share ; "There is insufficient publicity of its strongest qualities."

a6912.speaker: Ahmed Kellow, former CEO of Ethiopian Airlines
a6912.speech: Believes that many African airlines could benefit from intercontinental integration, as several have technical or infrastructure deficiencies: "Ethiopian can attract the most reliable types of partners" ; sees Ethiopian's business model as well-suited for partnerships with domestic carriers without compromising service delivery ; "Careful selection of routes with competitive advantages matters now," he told Fortune.

a6935.speaker: Vyacheslav Volodin, Chairman of the Russian State Duma
a6935.speech: Said that the US Agency for International Development (USAID) has become a criminal network operating in more than 100 countries and managing an annual budget of 50 to 60 billion dollars: "In accordance with its charter, USAID is supposed to support the economy, health care and education, as well as provide humanitarian responses. In fact, the agency has become a criminal network that operates in more than 100 countries and controls an annual budget of 50 to 60 billion dollars," the senior Russian legislator wrote on his Telegram channel ; "Today, USAID's headquarters in Washington has been closed and USAID is about to be dismantled. It is now important that those guilty of its crimes be punished and that this does not happen again," he stressed.

a6935.speaker: Vyacheslav Volodin, Chairman of the Russian State Duma
a6935.speech: Explained that the agency notably played a role in preparing coups d'état around the world, and that its so-called "democracy promotion" programmes harmed Ukraine, Georgia, Moldova, Armenia and a number of other countries; he revealed that over the last decade USAID spent more than 2 billion dollars in the former Soviet republics, of which "52% was allocated to Ukraine."

a6935.speaker: Vyacheslav Volodin, Chairman of the Russian State Duma
a6935.speech: Recalled that USAID also took part in funding research on biological weapons, and that a parliamentary inquiry conducted three years ago by the Duma into Pentagon projects to create and manage biological laboratories in Ukraine found that "the United States and personally [former US President Joe] Biden and his son [Hunter] are behind projects to develop and distribute weapons of mass destruction around the world"; according to him, Volodymyr Zelensky and Biden turned Ukrainian citizens into guinea pigs.

a6935.speaker: Russian State Duma parliamentary inquiry (cited)
a6935.speech: A parliamentary inquiry conducted three years ago by the Duma into the Pentagon's projects to create and manage biological laboratories in Ukraine revealed that "the United States and personally [former US President Joe] Biden and his son [Hunter] are behind projects to develop and distribute weapons of mass destruction around the world."

a6937.speaker: José Munice, HCB executive administrator for Production, Energy Transmission and Procurement
a6937.speech: Said, speaking to reporters, that the initiative to rehabilitate National Road N 301 is part of the 10-Year Vital Capex Project, which is aimed at developing a series of structural projects for the rehabilitation, modernization, and expansion of the HCB power plant, and that the investment aims to make the road robust enough to support the heavy vehicles that will transport equipment for the rehabilitation and modernization: "HCB, which celebrates its 50th anniversary this year, is developing a series of structural projects for the rehabilitation, modernization, and expansion of its power plant. The 10-Year Vital Capex Project is aimed at reversing the negative impact caused by the frequent maintenance of obsolete equipment."

a6937.speaker: José Munice, HCB executive administrator for Production, Energy Transmission and Procurement
a6937.speech: Said the 10-Year Vital CAPEX programme arises from a technical analysis of the equipment, after the infrastructure completed 50 years: "It was found that a significant portion of the equipment has been in operation for about 50 years, a fact that poses operational risks and so investment projects were developed to mitigate the risk."

a6937.speaker: José Munice, HCB executive administrator for Production, Energy Transmission and Procurement
a6937.speech: Highlighted the rehabilitation of the South Bank Power Station and the Songo and Matambo substations: "With the rehabilitation of the plant, the company foresees an increase in production capacity of 90 MW. With five generating units, we will replace the alternators, the turbines, the control systems, and the auxiliary systems, among others" ; on the Matambo Substation, responsible for distributing the energy generated by HCB to the central and northern regions of the country: "Here, we will also invest in modernizing and replacing some equipment that is already beyond its useful life" ; he also mentioned the proposed North Bank Power Station, which will be built alongside the existing power station, generating an additional 1,245 megawatts ; and on the solar project: "Among the projects is the construction of a 400 MW solar power plant planned for Matambo, Changara district, also in Tete province. The main objective of the solar power plant is to supply the energy deficit during the repair of the five turbines installed at HCB, one per year. Pre-feasibility studies for the project's implementation are already under way."

a6994.speaker: Russian presidential decree no. 711 of 20 August 2024 (official record)
a6994.speech: Appointed Tkachenko Vsevolod Igorevich as Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of the Russian Federation to the Republic of Kenya and Permanent Representative of the Russian Federation to the international organisations in Nairobi.

a6994.speaker: Libyan Presidential Council
a6994.speech: Adopted a decision to dismiss the governor and board of directors of the Central Bank of Libya, removing Sadiq Al-Kabir from his post, and appointed Muhammad Abdel Salam Al-Shukri, previously vice-president, as the new head of the central bank.

a6994.speaker: JNIM (“DNIM”) terrorists
a6994.speech: Declared full control of the Burkinabe army's positions in Djibo, in Soum province.

a6994.speaker: National Bank of Ethiopia
a6994.speech: Announced the introduction of a new system of daily monitoring of commercial banks as part of the financial reforms under way in the country.

a6994.speaker: Government of Burkina Faso
a6994.speech: Announced an investment of 117 million dollars in local rail production.

a6994.speaker: International Botanical Congress, Madrid
a6994.speech: A decision was taken to change, from 2026, the Latin names of more than 200 plants, fungi and algae containing cafr-, cafer-, caffr- and caffer-, dropping the letter “c”.

a7137.speaker: Dr. Ameenah Gurib-Fakim, former Mauritian President and chair of the Wise Council of ImpactHER
a7137.speech: Called for a radical shift in how Africa's role in global climate negotiations is perceived and represented, and urged a new narrative that redefines Africa's place in the climate equation: "A single company, NVIDIA, has a market capitalisation of 4.1 trillion dollars. The combined GDP of the entire African continent stands at 3.1 trillion." ; "Think about it in financial terms. When countries issue bonds, they pay coupons until maturity. In climate terms, it's as if Africa has subsidized a handful of countries without ever being repaid." ; stressed Africa contributes less than 4% of global greenhouse gas emissions yet remains among the regions most affected by climate change: "We are not asking for charity. We are not begging," rejecting the outdated aid-driven narrative surrounding Africa's climate position.

a7137.speaker: Dr. Ameenah Gurib-Fakim, former Mauritian President
a7137.speech: Addressed the growing weight of financial debt on African economies, noting, citing recent data, that the debt-to-GDP ratio in sub-Saharan Africa rose from 30% in 2013 to over 60% in 2022: "African countries that issue bonds must repay them in 10 years at high interest rates," contrasting this with developed nations' access to long-term, low-interest financing. "To avoid defaulting internationally, they default domestically - on health, education, and social safety nets."

a7137.speaker: Dr. Ameenah Gurib-Fakim, former Mauritian President
a7137.speech: Highlighted several structural contradictions: Africa imports over $50 billion in food annually despite possessing 60% of the world's arable land, and 600 million Africans still lack access to electricity; "Through the critical minerals we possess, Africa powers technologies developed elsewhere," underlining the continent's overlooked contribution to the Fourth Industrial Revolution ; lamented that nearly a decade after the Paris Agreement (COP21) Africa has yet to receive the promised technologies and tools needed to transition to green energy, and warned that without these, new environmental trade standards could penalise Africa before it even has the means to comply.

a7137.speaker: Dr. Ameenah Gurib-Fakim, former Mauritian President
a7137.speech: Advocated for debt restructuring, favoring extended repayment periods and fairer interest rates over blanket debt cancellation, and emphasised regional integration as a strategic imperative: "If African countries could come closer together, better coordination among a few influential states could accelerate economic integration and industrialisation." ; urged governments to mobilise sovereign resources, such as pension funds, to finance local development rather than relying exclusively on external capital.

a7137.speaker: Dr. Ameenah Gurib-Fakim, former Mauritian President
a7137.speech: Urged African media to take control of the continent's story: "When we create our own agencies, we shape the narrative," calling on journalists to focus on solutions and economic transformation rather than the usual depictions of poverty and crisis ; "Africa has been a victim of circumstance. But we are here to offer solutions." ; stressed the importance of African negotiators staying until the very end of international climate talks to ensure that "no decisions are made in their absence".

a7155.speaker: H.E. Dr. Jean Kaseya, Director-General, Africa CDC
